lessons.title: What Is iOS Development? Xcode and Your First iPhone App
lessons.metaTitle: iOS Development: Xcode and First App
lessons.description: Learn what an iOS developer does, what you need (a Mac and Xcode), how Swift and SwiftUI fit together, and how to build and run your first iPhone app.

content.text: An iOS developer builds apps for the iPhone, and often for the iPad, Apple Watch and other Apple devices too. The apps you use for banking, food delivery, travel, notes and fitness are mostly built by small teams who know one language, Swift, and one toolbox, Apple's frameworks. This course teaches that path from nothing to an app you can put on a phone and show to an employer. It is 15 lessons long, and from lesson 6 onwards we build one running project, an Expense Tracker.
Before the first line of code, it helps to know the map. You will see these names in job posts, so here is what each one means.

items: **Swift** is the main programming language for Apple platforms. It is modern, safe and readable. This is where you start.
**SwiftUI** is Apple's newer way to build screens. You describe what the screen should look like, and the system draws it. Most new apps and tutorials use it.
**UIKit** is the older screen toolkit. Many large companies still have apps built with it, so it is worth knowing later. Lesson 15 explains how the two live together.
**Objective-C** is the language that came before Swift. You can skip it at the start. You only need it if a job involves a very old code base.
**Xcode** is the free program from Apple where you write, run, test and publish apps.

content.text: What you need

The honest answer is a Mac. Xcode only runs on macOS, and you need it to build iOS apps. There is no complete way to build and publish native iPhone apps on Windows or Linux. If you do not own a Mac, think about a second-hand or refurbished one, or a cloud Mac rental for learning, and check the price against your budget before you start. You can still read the Swift lessons (2 to 5) on any computer, because the Swift language itself runs on other systems, but the app lessons need Xcode.

items: A Mac that can run a recent version of macOS and Xcode. Apple lists which Macs and system versions each Xcode release supports, so check their page before you install.
Enough free disk space. Xcode and its simulators are large, often tens of gigabytes.

An Apple ID, which is free. A free Apple ID is enough to run your own apps on the simulator, and Apple also allows limited testing on your own device. Publishing to the App Store needs a paid Apple Developer Program membership, and the price and rules are on Apple's site, so look there for the current details.

content.text: Everything in this course targets recent tools: Xcode 16 or newer and iOS 17 or newer. We pick iOS 17 as the lowest version because the modern state tools (the Observable macro) and SwiftData need it. Apple changes menus and templates with each Xcode release, so if a button has moved, search for the word in the menu bar. The ideas stay the same.
Install Xcode

items: Open the App Store on your Mac, search for **Xcode** and click Get. It is free, and the download is large, so start it early.
When it finishes, open Xcode once and accept the licence. It may offer to install extra components. Let it.
In Xcode, open **Settings** and look at the Platforms tab. Make sure an iOS simulator is installed. If not, download one there.

content.text: Create your first app

items: In Xcode choose **File > New > Project**.
Pick the **iOS** tab and then **App**. Click Next.
Product Name: `Hello`. Interface: **SwiftUI**. Language: **Swift**. If Xcode asks about storage or testing, leave the defaults for now. Click Next and save the project in a folder you can find later.
Xcode creates a project with a few files. Open the one called `ContentView.swift`.

content.text: The file contains a short piece of code. It looks a little like the one below, although the exact lines change a little between Xcode versions. You will understand every word of it by lesson 8, so for now just read it like a sentence.

The word `struct` makes a new type called `ContentView`. The `: View` after it says it is a screen piece. It must have a property called `body` that returns what to show. Here that is a **VStack**, a vertical stack, holding an icon and some text. The lines that start with a dot, such as `.padding()`, are **modifiers**, and they change how a view looks. The `#Preview` block at the bottom shows the screen live in Xcode, on the right side, without running the app. If you do not see it, choose **Editor > Canvas**.
Run it in the simulator

At the top of Xcode there is a device menu with names such as iPhone 16. Choose any recent iPhone and press the **Run** button, the triangle, or press Command and R. Xcode builds the app, starts the Simulator and opens your app on a pretend iPhone. The first run is slow, and later runs are quicker. Press the stop button when you are done.

Now make a change. Edit the text to your own name, and add a second `Text` line below it. Watch the preview update. This loop of change, see, change again is the heart of SwiftUI work, and it is much faster than the old way of building screens.
What is in the project folder

items: `HelloApp.swift` is the starting point. It has the `@main` mark, which tells the system where the app begins.
`ContentView.swift` is your first screen.
`Assets.xcassets` holds images, colours and the app icon.
The `.xcodeproj` file is the project itself. Open this file, not the folder, if you come back later.
If you ticked testing, there are folders for tests. We use them in lesson 14.

content.text: Habits that save time

items: Read Xcode's error messages. They appear as red marks beside the line number. Click one and read the full text. The first error often causes the others.
Use the preview for quick layout work and the simulator for real behaviour such as navigation.
Use Git from day one. In lesson 15 and on this site's Git course you will learn how. Xcode can create a Git repository when you create the project.
Keep one small project per idea. Do not worry about making it pretty yet.

content.text: Your task

items: Install Xcode and create an iOS App project called Hello with SwiftUI and Swift.
Change the text so it shows your name and one more line of your own.
Change the icon name to another one, for example `star.fill` or `heart.fill`, and change its colour.
Run it in the Simulator and take a screenshot, so you can see your progress at the end of the course.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The preview or the Simulator shows your own text and icon.
You can say in one sentence what Swift, SwiftUI and Xcode are.
You can say what a modifier is, using `.padding()` as an example.

steps.say: You write Swift and SwiftUI code in a file such as ContentView.swift.
Xcode checks the code and builds it into an app.
Xcode installs the app on the Simulator, a pretend iPhone on your Mac.
The screen shows what your code describes.

faqs.q: Can I learn iOS development without a Mac?
faqs.a: You can learn the Swift language on other systems, but building and running native iPhone apps needs Xcode, and Xcode only runs on macOS. A second-hand Mac or a cloud Mac is the usual route.

faqs.q: Should I learn Swift or Objective-C first?
faqs.a: Swift. It is the language Apple recommends for new work, and most tutorials and new apps use it. Objective-C is only needed for some older code bases.

faqs.q: Is SwiftUI or UIKit better for a beginner?
faqs.a: SwiftUI. It needs less code and updates in a live preview. UIKit is still used by many companies, so learn it after you are comfortable with SwiftUI.

quiz.q: What do you need to build native iPhone apps?
What is SwiftUI?
options: Apple's modern way to describe screens in code

quiz.q: What does a modifier such as .padding() do?
options: Returns a changed copy of a view

notes: iOS developer = builds iPhone apps. Main tools: Swift (language), SwiftUI (screens), Xcode (the program).
UIKit = older screen toolkit, still in many company apps. Objective-C = old language, skip at the start.
You need a Mac. Xcode runs only on macOS. Free Apple ID is enough for the Simulator.
App Store publishing needs the paid Apple Developer Program. Check Apple's site for the current price.
New project: File > New > Project > iOS > App, Interface SwiftUI, Language Swift.
A modifier (.padding(), .font()) returns a changed copy of a view. Run with Cmd+R.

lessons.title: Swift Basics: let, var, Types, if, switch and Loops
lessons.metaTitle: Swift Basics: let, var, Types and Loops
lessons.description: Learn how Swift stores values with let and var, its main types, string interpolation, arrays, dictionaries, and how to make decisions and repeat work.

content.text: Swift is the language behind every lesson from here on. In the next four lessons we learn it on its own, before we put it inside an app. You can practise in an Xcode **Playground** or in a small Command Line Tool project, or in the free Swift Playgrounds app. Pick whichever starts fastest. Each example prints its answer with `print`, so you can see what it does.
let and var

Swift has two ways to give a name to a value. Use `let` for a **constant**, a value that never changes after you set it. Use `var` for a **variable**, a value you will change later. Prefer `let` whenever you can. Swift even warns you when a `var` is never changed. It is a small habit that prevents many bugs, because a value that cannot change cannot be changed by mistake.

let name = "Asha"
var score = 10
score = score + 5
print("\(name) has \(score) points")

Swift works out the type by itself, which is called **type inference**. Here `name` is a `String` and `score` is an `Int`. You can also write the type on purpose, with a colon: `let price: Double = 4`. This is useful when the number should be a decimal even though you typed a whole number.

The special part in the print line is `\(name)`. A backslash followed by brackets inside a string drops a value into the text. This is called **string interpolation**, and you will use it all the time.
The main types

items: `Int` is a whole number such as 42. `Double` is a decimal number such as 3.14. Use `Double` for ordinary decimals in this course.
`String` is text. `Bool` is `true` or `false`.
Swift will not mix types by itself. `Int` plus `Double` is an error until you convert one: `Double(score) + 2.5`. This is strict on purpose, and it catches mistakes before the app runs.

Money needs care. A `Double` cannot hold some decimal values exactly, so real finance apps use the `Decimal` type. We use `Double` in the course to keep the code short, and the Expense Tracker lesson says so again.

content.text: Arrays and dictionaries
An **array** is an ordered list of values of one type. A **dictionary** keeps pairs, a key and a value, and you look up a value by its key.

var expenses: [Double] = [12.5, 40, 7.25]
expenses.append(19.99)
print(expenses.count)        // 4
print(expenses[0])           // 12.5, counting starts at zero

var limits: [String: Double] = ["Food": 200, "Travel": 150]
limits["Fun"] = 80
print(limits["Food"] ?? 0)   // 200.0

Notice that looking up `limits["Food"]` gives an *optional* value, because the key might not exist. The `?? 0` part says *use zero if there is nothing*. Optionals are so important that lesson 5 is all about them.
Making decisions: if and switch

Use `if` to choose between paths. The conditions do not need brackets, but the braces are required. Use `switch` when one value can match many cases. A `switch` in Swift must cover every possible case, so the compiler warns you if you forget one.
The pattern `3...5` is a **range** that includes 3, 4 and 5. The range `0..<5` stops before 5. Both are very common in loops.
Repeating work: loops

A `for` loop walks through a list or a range. A `while` loop repeats as long as a condition is true, so be sure something inside it changes, or it never ends. You will use `for` much more than `while`.
Common beginner mistakes

items: Changing a `let` constant. Swift stops you with an error. Change it to `var` only if the value really must change.
Forgetting that array counting starts at 0. The first item is `items[0]`, and asking for an index that does not exist crashes the program.
Mixing `Int` and `Double` in one sum. Convert with `Double(x)`.
Writing `=` when you mean `==`. One stores a value. Two compare.

content.text: Your task

items: Create a Playground or a command line project.
Make an array of five expense amounts and use a `for` loop to add them into a `var total`.
Print `Over budget` if the total is above 100 and `Within budget` otherwise.
Make a dictionary of three category names and limits, and print each one with string interpolation.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your total is right when you add the numbers by hand.
Changing one amount changes the message when it crosses 100.
You can say the difference between `let` and `var` and why `let` is the better first choice.

steps.say: let creates a constant. Once it is set, Swift will not let you change it.
var creates a variable. You can give it a new value later.
Swift works out the type of each name and checks every use.
print shows the result in the console, with values dropped into the text.

faqs.q: Should I use let or var?
faqs.a: Start with let. Change to var only when the value really has to change. Swift will warn you when a var is never changed.

faqs.q: Why does Swift not allow Int plus Double?
faqs.a: Swift is strict about types so mistakes show up when you build the app and not when a user runs it. Convert on purpose, for example with Double(count).

faqs.q: Do I need a Mac to practise Swift?
faqs.a: For the language alone, no, because Swift also runs on other systems. For the app lessons you need Xcode on a Mac.

quiz.q: Which keyword makes a value that cannot change after it is set?
quiz.explain: Prefer let, and use var only when the value must change.

quiz.q: What does string interpolation look like in Swift?
Why does Swift refuse to add an Int and a Double directly?
options: It is strict about types so mistakes are caught early
quiz.explain: Convert on purpose, for example Double(count).

notes: `let` = constant, cannot change. `var` = variable, can change. Prefer `let`.
Swift works out types itself (type inference). Int + Double needs a conversion: `Double(x)`.
Interpolation: `"Hello \(name)"` drops a value into text.
Array: ordered list, first item is `[0]`. Dictionary: key and value pairs, lookup gives an optional.
`if`, `else if`, `switch` (must cover every case). Ranges: `1...3` includes 3, `0..<3` stops before 3.
`for item in list` walks a list. `while` repeats while a condition is true.

lessons.title: Swift Functions and Closures: map, filter and reduce
lessons.description: Learn to write Swift functions with argument labels and default values, then closures, trailing closure syntax and the map, filter, sorted and reduce helpers.

content.text: A **function** is a named piece of code that you can run whenever you need it. A **closure** is a function without a name that you can pass around like a value. SwiftUI uses both on nearly every line, so this lesson is time well spent. We keep the Expense Tracker idea: amounts of money and what we do with them.
Writing a function

A function starts with `func`, then a name, then its inputs in brackets, then an arrow and the type it gives back. Swift functions have a special habit: each input has an **argument label** that you write when you call the function. This makes calls read like short sentences.

Look at `total(of amounts:)`. The first word, `of`, is the label used when you call it. The second word, `amounts`, is the name used inside the function. If you do not want a label, write an underscore: `func total(_ amounts: [Double])`. Then you call `total([1, 2])`. If a function gives nothing back, you leave out the arrow.
Default values
An input can have a default. Callers may then leave it out. This keeps simple calls short and still allows detail when you need it.

`String(format:)` comes from Apple's Foundation library. It works with the usual percent codes such as `%.2f` for two decimals. For text a user will see, SwiftUI has better tools for currency, and lesson 9 uses one. Currency symbols and number formats differ by country, so do not hard-code them in a real app.
Closures
A closure is a block of code in curly braces. Its inputs come first, followed by the word `in`. You can store it in a constant, pass it to a function, or return it.

Look at the last call. When the last input of a function is a closure, you can write the closure *after* the brackets. This is called a **trailing closure**. You will see this shape in SwiftUI all the time, for example in `Button("Add") { ... }`, where the braces hold the code that runs when someone taps.
map, filter, sorted and reduce
Arrays have helpers that take a closure. They replace many small loops, and they read as a description of what you want.

items: `map` makes a new array by changing each item.
`filter` keeps only the items for which the closure says true.
`sorted` puts the items in order. The closure says which of two items comes first.
`reduce` folds all items into one value. The first input is the starting value, here 0.
`$0` and `$1` are short names for the first and second inputs. They are fine for tiny closures. When a closure grows, give the inputs real names, because the code is easier to read later.

content.text: Functions inside types

When a function lives inside a struct or class, it is called a **method**. In the next lesson you will put `total` inside a type that holds expenses. Closures also *capture* the values they use from the code around them. This is powerful, and also the reason that, in classes, you sometimes meet the words `[weak self]` in longer examples. We come back to this when it matters.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the argument label when you call a function. Swift's error message names the missing label.
Writing a very long closure on one line. Split it onto several lines with named inputs.
Using `reduce` when a plain loop would be clearer. Choose the one a teammate would understand fastest.

content.text: Your task

items: Write `average(of:)` that takes an array of `Double` and returns the average. Return 0 for an empty array.
Write `isLarge(_:limit:)` with a default limit of 50 that returns a `Bool`.
Given an array of amounts, use `filter` to keep those above 20, then `map` to add 10 per cent, then `reduce` to total them.
Call your own function with a trailing closure, like `repeatTask` above.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `average(of: [10, 20, 30])` prints 20.0 and `average(of: [])` prints 0.0.
You can explain what `$0` means.
You can say what a trailing closure is and find one in the examples.

steps.say: You start with an array of values.
filter keeps only the values that pass your test.
map changes each remaining value into a new one.
reduce folds the list into one value, such as a total.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a function and a closure?
faqs.a: A function has a name. A closure is a block of code without a name that you can store in a constant or pass to another function. Functions are really a special kind of closure.

faqs.q: What does $0 mean in Swift?
faqs.a: It is a short name for the first input of a closure. $1 is the second. Use them for tiny closures and write real names when the closure grows.

faqs.q: What is a trailing closure?
faqs.a: When the last input of a function is a closure, you can write it in braces after the brackets. SwiftUI buttons and lists use this style all the time.

quiz.q: What is a trailing closure?
options: A closure written in braces after the brackets when it is the last input

quiz.q: What does $0 mean inside a closure?
options: The first input of the closure

quiz.q: Which array helper changes every item into a new value?
quiz.explain: filter keeps items, sorted orders them, reduce folds them into one value.

notes: Function: `func name(label input: Type) -> Result`. The label is used when you call it.
Use `_` to remove a label. A default value (`currency: String = "$"`) lets callers skip it.
Closure = code in braces, inputs then `in`. Trailing closure: write it after the brackets.
`map` changes each item. `filter` keeps some. `sorted` orders. `reduce` folds to one value.
`$0` and `$1` are short names for closure inputs. Use real names when the closure is long.
A function inside a struct or class is called a method.

lessons.title: Swift Structs, Classes, Enums and Protocols Explained
lessons.description: Understand value types and reference types, how to model data with structs and enums, share behaviour with protocols, and add features with extensions.

content.text: Real apps hold real things: an expense, a user, a recipe. Swift gives you several ways to model them. Picking the right one is a skill, and it is a very common interview topic. This lesson builds the data model that the Expense Tracker uses later.
Structs

A **struct** groups related values and the functions that work on them. You make a new one by calling its name with the values. Swift gives every struct a free **memberwise initializer**, so you do not have to write the set-up code yourself.

Notice the function `summary()` has no `return`. When a function body is a single expression, Swift returns it for you. Also, `lunch` is a `let`, so none of its properties can change. If you need to change one, declare it with `var`.
Value types and reference types

This is the idea to understand well. Structs are **value types**. When you assign a struct to a new name, or pass it to a function, you get your own *copy*. Changing the copy does not change the original. Classes are **reference types**. A copy of a class variable points to the *same* object, so a change through one name shows up through the other.

struct PointS { var x = 0 }
class PointC { var x = 0 }

var a = PointS(); var b = a
b.x = 5
print(a.x, b.x)     // 0 5, two separate copies

let c = PointC(); let d = c
d.x = 5
print(c.x, d.x)     // 5 5, one shared object

items: Use a **struct** by default. Copies are easy to reason about, and SwiftUI is built around structs.
Use a **class** when you need one shared object that many parts of the code change, or when a framework requires it. Classes can also inherit from other classes, which structs cannot do.
A class needs an `init` that sets every property, unless all of them have default values.
A struct that must change its own properties inside a method marks that method `mutating`.

content.text: Enums
An **enum** is a type with a fixed set of cases. It is perfect for things that can be one of a few options, such as an expense category. Cases can even carry extra values.

`CaseIterable` gives you `allCases`, a list of every case, which is ideal for building a picker. The `LoadState` enum is a very common pattern. One value tells a screen whether to show a spinner, a list or an error message, and the `switch` makes you handle every case.
Protocols

A **protocol** is a list of requirements, the properties and methods a type must have. Any type that meets the list can say it *conforms* to the protocol. Code that asks for the protocol does not care which type it receives, as long as the type can do the job.

Two protocols appear in SwiftUI work again and again. `Identifiable` says a type has a stable `id`, so a list can tell items apart. `Codable` lets a type turn into and out of JSON, which is lesson 11. Protocols also make testing easier, because you can swap a real part for a simple fake one in lesson 13.
Extensions
An **extension** adds new methods or computed properties to a type that already exists, even one you did not write. It is a tidy way to keep code grouped.
Choosing between them

items: Data that describes a thing: a struct.
One of a few options: an enum.
A shared object with its own life, such as a manager that many screens use: a class.
A promise of behaviour, so different types can be swapped: a protocol.

content.text: Your task

items: Make an `Expense` struct with `id` (a `UUID()`), `title`, `amount` and a `Category` enum. Make it conform to `Identifiable`.
Write an extension on `Array<Expense>` with a `total` property.
Prove the difference between a struct and a class copy with your own tiny example, and write one sentence about what you saw.
Make an enum `LoadState` and a function that returns a message for each case.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your `total` property adds up amounts correctly.
Changing a copy of the struct leaves the original unchanged, and changing a copy of the class changes both.
You can say when you would choose a struct and when a class.

steps.say: A struct is a value type. Assigning it makes a new copy.
Changing the copy leaves the original alone, so structs are easy to reason about.
A class is a reference type. Assigning it points to the same object.
A change made through any name shows up everywhere, so use classes on purpose.

faqs.q: Should I use a struct or a class in Swift?
faqs.a: Use a struct by default. Choose a class when you need one shared object with its own life, inheritance, or when a framework needs it.

faqs.q: What is a protocol in Swift?
faqs.a: A list of properties and methods that a type promises to have. Code that asks for the protocol works with any type that meets it, which helps with flexibility and testing.

faqs.q: What is an enum used for?
faqs.a: For a value that can be only one of a fixed set of cases, such as a category or a loading state. Cases can carry extra data.

quiz.q: You assign a struct to a new variable and change the copy. What happens to the original?
quiz.explain: Structs are value types, so each name has its own copy.

quiz.q: Which type is best for a value that can be only one of a few options?
What is a protocol?
options: A list of properties and methods a type promises to have

notes: Struct = value type: assigning makes a copy. Class = reference type: assigning shares one object.
Use a struct by default. Use a class for one shared object, inheritance, or when a framework needs it.
Enum = fixed set of cases, can carry values. `CaseIterable` gives `allCases`.
Protocol = list of requirements a type promises. Identifiable (has id) and Codable (JSON) are common.
Extension = add methods or computed properties to an existing type.
A struct method that changes the struct is marked `mutating`.

lessons.title: Swift Optionals and Error Handling: if let, guard and try
lessons.description: Learn why Swift has optionals, how to unwrap them safely with if let, guard let and ??, and how to throw, catch and handle errors with do, try and catch.

content.text: Optionals are the Swift feature that surprises people most, and the one that makes Swift apps crash less often. Many languages have a value called `null` or `nil` that sneaks into your code and crashes it later. Swift makes the possibility of *no value* part of the type, so the compiler makes you deal with it before the app runs. This lesson also covers errors, the other thing that can go wrong in real apps.
What an optional is

An **optional** is a box that holds either a value or nothing. You write it by adding a question mark to a type. `Int?` means *an Int, or nothing*. The nothing is written `nil`. A plain `Int` can never be `nil`.

var age: Int? = nil
print(age)          // nil
age = 30
print(age)          // Optional(30)

let text = "42"
let number = Int(text)     // Int? because the text might not be a number
print(number)              // Optional(42)
print(Int("abc"))          // nil

`Int(text)` is a good example. Not every piece of text is a number, so the result is an optional. You cannot use an `Int?` where an `Int` is needed until you open the box, and Swift gives several safe ways to do that.
Unwrapping safely

items: `if let` is best when you only want to do something extra if a value is there.
`guard let` is best at the top of a function. It keeps the main path of the code flat and easy to read, and the `else` part must leave with `return`, `throw` or similar.
`??` is best when there is a sensible default.
`?.` is best when you want to read through a chain, and a missing link should simply give `nil`.

content.text: The danger of the exclamation mark

Adding `!` after an optional is called **force unwrapping**. It says *I promise this is not nil*. If you are wrong, the app crashes at once. People use it in examples to keep them short, and then in real code to get past an error message. Avoid it. A crash is the worst experience for a user, and it is also very easy to avoid. The few places where `!` is acceptable, such as a value that your own set-up has already filled in, should be rare and you should be able to explain each one.
Errors: throw, try and catch

Not every problem is a missing value. A file may not open. A web call may fail. A user may type an amount below zero. Swift uses **errors** for these. An error is a value of any type that conforms to the `Error` protocol, usually an enum. A function that can fail is marked `throws`, and the caller must write `try` before it.

A `do` block runs the risky code. If anything inside throws, Swift jumps to the first matching `catch`. The last bare `catch` handles everything else, and inside it a value called `error` is available. You also meet two shortcuts: `try?` gives an optional (`nil` if it failed) and `try!` crashes on failure, so treat it like the exclamation mark.
Errors or optionals?

items: When *nothing there* is a normal answer, such as looking up a key, use an optional.
When something *went wrong* and the caller should know why, throw an error.
When you build a screen, turn errors into something a person can read. A friendly message and a way to try again beat a technical text.

content.text: In lesson 11 you will meet `Result`, an enum with a success case and a failure case, and `async` functions that throw. They work in the same way as what you learned here.
Your task

items: Write `parseAmount(_ text: String) -> Double?` using `Double(text)`. Test it with `"12.5"` and `"abc"`.
Write a function with `guard let` that prints a greeting only when a name is given.
Add a `ExpenseError.tooLarge` case and make `makeExpense` throw it when the amount is over 10,000.
Catch each error in a `do` block and print a clear message.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `parseAmount("abc")` gives `nil` and does not crash.
Each bad input to `makeExpense` prints its own message.
You can name three safe ways to unwrap an optional and say why `!` is risky.

steps.say: An optional holds a value or nothing. The type says so with a question mark.
if let and guard let open the box and check it before you use it.
When there is a value, your code runs with a plain, safe value.
When it is nil, the else path or a default with ?? takes over, and the app does not crash.

faqs.q: What is an optional in Swift?
faqs.a: A type that holds either a value or nothing (nil). It is written with a question mark, such as Int?. The compiler makes you handle the nil case before you use the value.

faqs.q: What is the difference between if let and guard let?
faqs.a: Both unwrap an optional safely. if let uses the value inside its braces. guard let makes the value usable for the rest of the function and must leave the function in its else part.

faqs.q: When should I use try? and try!?
faqs.a: try? turns a failure into nil, which is fine when you do not need the reason. try! crashes if the call fails, so avoid it in real code.

quiz.q: What does Int? mean?
options: An Int that is always positive

quiz.q: Which is the safest way to use an optional you are not sure about?
quiz.explain: Force unwrapping crashes the app if the value is nil.

quiz.q: A function marked throws is called with…

notes: Optional: `Int?` is an Int or nothing (`nil`). `Int("abc")` gives nil.
Safe unwrap: `if let`, `guard let` (leave early), `??` default, `?.` chaining.
`!` force unwrap crashes the app on nil. Avoid it.
Errors: a type that conforms to `Error`, usually an enum. A function that can fail is `throws`.
Call with `try` inside `do { } catch { }`. `try?` gives nil on failure. `try!` crashes.
Nothing there = optional. Something went wrong = throw an error.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Views, Modifiers and Stacks: Build a Layout
lessons.description: Learn how SwiftUI builds screens from small views, how modifiers and their order change the result, and how VStack, HStack, ZStack and Spacer lay things out.

content.text: From this lesson on we build screens. SwiftUI has one big idea: a screen is a *function of its data*. You describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and SwiftUI redraws it whenever the data changes. You do not move buttons around by hand. This is called **declarative** UI, and it is the reason SwiftUI code is short.
Everything is a view

A **view** is a small piece of the screen: some text, an image, a button, a list, or a group of other views. A view is a struct that follows the `View` protocol and has a `body` property. The word `some View` means *a view of some kind, and the compiler works out which*. Views are cheap, so SwiftUI expects you to make many small ones and combine them.

Read it from the outside in. An `HStack` puts things side by side. It holds an icon, a `VStack` with two lines of text, a `Spacer` and the amount. The `Spacer` is a flexible gap that pushes the amount to the right edge. `Image(systemName:)` uses **SF Symbols**, thousands of free icons that come with Apple's systems. The Mac app named SF Symbols lets you browse them. `Text(amount, format: .currency(code: "USD"))` shows a number as money, and the currency code is a parameter, so you can change it.
The three stacks

items: `VStack` lays views out **vertically**, top to bottom.
`HStack` lays views out **horizontally**, left to right. In languages that read right to left, SwiftUI flips this for you.
`ZStack` layers views **on top of each other**, with the first at the back. Use it for a badge on an image, or text over a colour.
Each stack takes `alignment` and `spacing`. `Spacer()` takes up all the space it can. `Divider()` draws a thin line.

content.text: Modifiers

A **modifier** is a method that returns a changed copy of a view: `.font`, `.padding`, `.background`, `.frame`, `.foregroundStyle`, `.cornerRadius` and many more. You chain them, one after another. The surprise for beginners is that **the order matters**, because each modifier wraps the result of the one before it.

// Background first, then padding: the yellow stays tight around the text.
Text("Hello")
    .background(.yellow)
    .padding()

// Padding first, then background: the yellow includes the padding.
Text("Hello")
    .padding()
    .background(.yellow)

Try both in the preview and look at the difference. When a layout looks wrong, the order of modifiers is the first thing to check. Some modifiers, such as `.font`, pass down to every view inside a stack, so you can set a font once on a `VStack` and not on each line.
Frames, sizes and safe areas

Views take as little space as they need. Use `.frame(width:height:)` for a fixed size, or `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` to stretch to the full width. A screen on an iPhone has **safe areas**, the parts not hidden by the notch, the rounded corners or the home bar. SwiftUI keeps your content inside them by default, which is what you want for text. A background colour often should go behind them, and `.ignoresSafeArea()` lets it.
Small views are a good habit

items: When a `body` is longer than about 30 lines, cut a piece out into its own struct, like `ExpenseRow` above. Smaller views are easier to read and to preview.
Give a view only the data it needs, in `let` properties. That makes it easy to reuse and to test with a preview.

Use **semantic** styles such as `.font(.headline)` and `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)`, and not fixed sizes and colours. They adapt to Dark Mode and to people who set larger text in their phone's settings, which is part of making an app accessible.

content.text: Colours, fonts and sizes you pick should still look right in Dark Mode and with larger text. In Xcode's preview you can switch both on, and it takes a minute. It is a habit worth building from the start, and it matters for accessibility.
Common mistakes

items: A view with more than ten direct children in one stack. Group them with `Group` or split them into smaller views.
Forgetting that `Spacer` only expands inside a stack.
Fixed frame sizes for text. A bigger font makes the text cut off.

content.text: Your task

items: Create a new SwiftUI file called `ExpenseRow.swift` with the row above and change the icon and colours.
Create `SummaryCard` and show it above the row inside a `VStack` in `ContentView`.
Swap the order of `.padding()` and `.background()` and write down what changes.
Turn on Dark Mode and a larger text size in the preview, and fix anything that looks wrong.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The row shows an icon on the left, two lines of text, and the amount pushed to the right edge.
You can explain why modifier order matters with an example.
Your screen still looks fine in Dark Mode.

steps.say: You start with a simple view such as Text.
Each modifier returns a new view that wraps the one before it. Padding adds space around the text.
The background then paints the padded area as well. Swap them and the yellow shrinks.
What you see depends on the order of the modifiers, so read them from top to bottom.

faqs.q: What is a view in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: A small piece of the screen, written as a struct with a body property. Views are cheap, so you combine many small ones into a screen.

faqs.q: Why does modifier order matter in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: Each modifier wraps the result of the one before it. Padding then background paints the padded area, while background then padding paints only the content.

faqs.q: What is an SF Symbol?
faqs.a: One of thousands of free icons built into Apple systems, used with Image(systemName:). The SF Symbols app from Apple lets you browse them.

quiz.q: Which stack puts views side by side?
quiz.explain: VStack is vertical and ZStack layers views on top of each other.

quiz.q: Why does the order of modifiers matter?
options: Each modifier wraps the result of the one before it
Swift runs them backwards by random

quiz.q: What does Spacer() do inside a stack?
options: Takes up the free space and pushes views apart

notes: SwiftUI: describe the screen for the current data. It redraws when data changes.
View = struct with a `body`. Make many small views.
VStack = top to bottom. HStack = side by side. ZStack = layers. `Spacer()` takes free space.
Modifier order matters: each one wraps the one before. `.padding().background()` is not the same as the reverse.
SF Symbols: free icons, `Image(systemName: "cart.fill")`.
Use semantic styles (`.headline`, `.secondary`) so Dark Mode and larger text work.

lessons.title: SwiftUI State and Binding: @State, Button and TextField
lessons.description: Learn how SwiftUI remembers data with @State, shares it with child views through @Binding, and connects buttons, text fields and toggles with the dollar sign.

content.text: A screen that never changes is only a picture. To react to taps and typing, SwiftUI needs a place to keep changing data. That place is **state**. The rule of SwiftUI is simple and strict: *when state changes, the views that read it are drawn again*. You never say *update this label*. You only change the data.
@State

A view is a struct, and structs are values that SwiftUI creates and throws away often. So an ordinary `var` inside a view would be lost. Putting `@State` in front of a property tells SwiftUI to keep that value safely for the life of the view and to redraw the view when it changes. By habit, state is `private`, because the view that owns it is the one that changes it.

The closure after `Button("Add one")` is the code that runs on a tap. It changes `count`. SwiftUI sees the change and draws the `Text` again with the new number. There is no other step. Notice `role: .destructive`, which makes the button red, because a button that throws things away should look different.
The dollar sign: bindings

A text field must both *show* a value and *change* it when the user types. A plain value cannot do the second job. A **binding** is a two-way connection to a value that lives somewhere else. You make one from a state property by putting a dollar sign in front of its name.

items: `title` (no dollar sign) is the value. Use it to *read*.
`$title` is a binding. Use it to let another view *read and write* the same value, as `TextField` and `Toggle` do.
As you type, the text field writes to `title`, SwiftUI notices, and the `Text` below updates on each key press.

content.text: @Binding: sharing state with a child view

When you split a form into smaller views, the child needs to change the parent's data. Give the child a `@Binding` property. The parent passes `$value`, and the child reads and writes it, without owning it. There is still only one real copy of the data, which is why the parent and child can never disagree.
Turning text into a number

A text field holds a `String`, but an amount is a `Double`. Lesson 5 gave you the tool: `Double(amountText)` returns an optional. Use it to decide whether the form is valid, and disable the button when it is not.

Decimal separators differ by country. Some regions type a comma, and `Double("4,5")` is `nil`. For a real app, prefer `TextField("Amount", value: $amount, format: .number)` with a `Double` state, which follows the user's region. We keep the text version here so you can see how the pieces connect.
What should be state?

items: Data that changes and that the screen shows: a counter, a text field's text, whether a sheet is open.
Not data that can be worked out from other state. A total is a *computed property*, not a second state value. Two copies of one fact can go out of step.
Keep state as low as you can and as local as you can. If two views need to change it, put it in their nearest shared parent and pass a binding.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Changing a `var` property that has no `@State`. The screen does not update, and Xcode may refuse to compile it.
Forgetting the dollar sign in `TextField(text: title)`. The error says it expected a `Binding<String>`.
Putting state in a child view when the parent also needs it.

content.text: Your task

items: Build `CounterView` and add a button that subtracts one but never goes below zero.
Build the form with title, amount and a toggle, and show a live summary line under it.
Move the amount field into its own view with `@Binding`.
Disable the Add button until the title is not empty and the amount is above zero.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Typing in the field updates the summary line on every key press.
The button turns on only when the form is valid.
You can say what `@State`, `$title` and `@Binding` each do.

steps.say: The user taps a button or types in a field.
Your code changes a @State value. You only change data, never the label.
SwiftUI notices that a value used by the view has changed.
The view body runs again and the screen shows the new value.

faqs.q: What does @State do in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: It tells SwiftUI to keep a value safely for the life of the view and to redraw the view whenever the value changes. State is usually private to the view that owns it.

faqs.q: What does the dollar sign mean in $title?
faqs.a: It makes a binding, a two-way link to the value, so a control such as a TextField can both show it and change it.

faqs.q: When do I use @Binding?
faqs.a: When a child view needs to change data that is owned by its parent. The parent passes $value and the child declares @Binding, so there is still only one copy of the data.

quiz.q: What does @State do?
options: Saves a value on the server
Keeps a value for the view and redraws the view when it changes

quiz.q: What does the dollar sign in $title give you?
options: A binding, a two-way link to the value

quiz.q: A child view must change a value owned by its parent. What does it declare?

notes: `@State private var x` = SwiftUI keeps the value and redraws the view when it changes.
You change data, never the label. State changes then the screen follows.
`$x` = binding, a two-way link. TextField and Toggle need one.
`@Binding` in a child view = reads and writes the parent's value. Only one real copy of the data.
Do not store a total as state. Compute it from other state.
`Double("4,5")` is nil in some regions. `TextField(value:format:)` follows the user's region.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Lists, NavigationStack and Sheets
lessons.description: Build a list screen with List and ForEach, move to a detail screen with NavigationStack, open an add screen in a sheet, and let users swipe to delete.

content.text: Almost every app is a list that leads to detail screens. In this lesson the Expense Tracker gets its first real structure: a list of expenses, a detail screen for each, and a sheet to add a new one. For now the data lives in memory, so it disappears when you close the app. Lesson 12 fixes that with SwiftData.
The model

A list needs to tell its rows apart, so each row needs a stable identity. We make the model `Identifiable`, with a `UUID` as the `id`. We also add `Hashable`, which navigation needs to remember which item was picked. A struct whose properties are all `Hashable` gets this for free.
List and ForEach

`List` shows rows that scroll, with the usual iPhone look. If you give it an array of identifiable items, it makes one row per item. Use `ForEach` inside a `List` when you want extras such as swipe to delete, or when the list has sections.
Take the pieces one at a time.

items: **`NavigationStack`** is the container for a stack of screens. It gives you the title bar and the back button for free.

**`NavigationLink(value:)`** makes a row tappable and says *which item was chosen*. The matching **`navigationDestination(for:)`** says *which screen to show for that kind of item*. This pairing keeps navigation tidy even in big apps.
**`.onDelete`** adds swipe to delete on a `ForEach`. SwiftUI gives you the positions to remove.
**`.toolbar`** places buttons in the navigation bar. A `Button` with a `systemImage` shows an icon and keeps its text for accessibility.
**`.sheet(isPresented:)`** slides a screen up from the bottom while the boolean is true. Because we pass `$showAdd`, the sheet can set it back to false when it closes.

content.text: The detail screen
The sheet that adds an expense

The sheet needs to hand the new expense back. A simple way is to pass a closure, a function the sheet calls when the user taps Save. The sheet also uses the `dismiss` action from the environment to close itself. `@Environment` reads values the system provides, such as the dismiss action, the colour scheme or the text size.

Older tutorials use `NavigationView` and `NavigationLink(destination:)`. Both still work but are deprecated for new code. Use `NavigationStack`, as above. If you see the older names, the idea is the same.
How the pieces fit together

Follow one tap through the code to see why it works. The user taps a row. The `NavigationLink` hands the chosen `Expense` to the `NavigationStack`. The stack looks for a `navigationDestination` that accepts the type `Expense`, builds `ExpenseDetailView` with that value and pushes it on screen. Pressing back removes it again. Nothing in the list needs to know what the detail screen looks like, and the detail screen does not need to know where the user came from. This separation is the reason value-based navigation scales to large apps, and also the reason a deep link or a saved navigation path can open any screen later.

The same thinking applies to the sheet. The list owns the boolean `showAdd` and the array. The sheet owns only what the user is typing. It gives back one finished value through the closure, and the list decides what to do with it. Each view has one job and a clear way to talk to its neighbours, and that is what makes the screens easy to change one at a time.
Common mistakes

items: An array of items without a stable `id`, or with an `id` that changes each time. Rows jump around or lose their state.
Putting a `NavigationLink` inside another navigation container by accident, which makes two title bars.
Forgetting that the data here is only in memory. Close the app and it resets. That is expected until lesson 12.

content.text: Your task

items: Type the three views into your project and run the app.
Add a category `Picker` to the sheet using `ForEach(Category.allCases, id: \.self)`.
Show the total of all expenses at the top of the list in a `Section`.
Add an empty state: when the array is empty, show a `Text("No expenses yet")` instead of a blank list.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Tapping a row opens the detail screen and the back button returns.
The sheet adds a new row and closes. Swiping a row deletes it.
You can explain what `NavigationLink(value:)` and `navigationDestination(for:)` do together.

steps.say: A List shows one row for each item in your array.
Tapping a row sends the chosen item through its NavigationLink.
navigationDestination decides which screen belongs to that type of item.
The detail screen opens with the item, and the back button comes for free.

faqs.q: What is the difference between List and ForEach?
faqs.a: List is the scrolling container with the standard look. ForEach makes views from a collection and works inside List, which lets you add swipe to delete or sections.

faqs.q: Should I use NavigationView or NavigationStack?
faqs.a: NavigationStack. NavigationView is deprecated for new code. NavigationStack supports value-based links and programmatic navigation.

faqs.q: Why must list items be Identifiable?
faqs.a: SwiftUI needs a stable id for each row to know which row is which when data changes. Identifiable types provide that id, and a UUID is a simple way to make one.

quiz.q: Which container gives you the title bar and back button for a stack of screens?
quiz.explain: NavigationView is deprecated for new code.

quiz.q: Why must list items be Identifiable?
options: To make them faster to type
SwiftUI needs a stable id to tell rows apart

quiz.q: Which modifier adds swipe to delete to a ForEach?

notes: Model: `Identifiable` (stable id) and `Hashable` for value-based navigation.
`List` + `ForEach(items)` makes one row per item. `.onDelete` adds swipe to delete.
`NavigationStack` = title bar and back button. `NavigationLink(value:)` + `.navigationDestination(for:)` pick the screen.
`.sheet(isPresented: $show)` slides a screen up. Close it with `@Environment(\.dismiss)`.
Pass a closure (`onSave`) to hand the new item back to the list.
NavigationView is deprecated for new code. Use NavigationStack.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Forms, Pickers, Validation and Animation
lessons.description: Build a proper settings-style form with Picker and DatePicker, check the input before saving, show errors clearly, and add smooth animation with withAnimation.

content.text: The add screen from lesson 8 works, but it looks plain, and a user could save an empty title or a negative amount. In this lesson we replace it with a real form, check the input, and add a little motion so changes feel natural and not abrupt. These are the finishing touches that make an app feel made with care.
Form and Section

`Form` is a container that gives its content the grouped, settings-app look, and it adapts to the platform. Inside it, `Section` groups related rows under a header and a footer. Controls inside a form pick up the right spacing for free.
There is a lot here, so here is what to notice.

items: **`Picker`** needs a binding to the selected value and a list of choices. Each choice has a `tag` that matches the type of the selection. With an enum that conforms to `CaseIterable`, `ForEach(Category.allCases)` builds the whole list for you.
**`DatePicker`** gives the native date control. `displayedComponents: .date` hides the time.

**`TextField(value:format:)`** edits a number directly, and it follows the user's region for decimal marks. It replaces the `Double(text)` step from lesson 7. The field shows `0` at first, and in a real app you may prefer an optional state value or a placeholder.
**`if let titleError`** is the short form of unwrapping that works in modern Swift. It shows the message only when there is one.

**Validation** lives in small computed properties, and a `save()` function checks them. We show errors only after the first try to save, so the form does not shout at someone who has not typed anything yet.

content.text: Good form habits

items: Say what is wrong in plain words and next to the field, not in a pop-up.
Do the checks again where the data is saved, not only on the screen. In lesson 14 you will test the same rules without any screen.
Never rely on a field's keyboard type to keep out bad input. People can paste.
Mark which fields are optional.

content.text: Accessibility of forms

A form is where accessibility matters most, because people must read labels and enter data. Give every field a visible label or a clear placeholder. The built-in controls already work with VoiceOver, Apple's screen reader, and with larger text sizes, so avoid replacing them with custom ones unless you need to. When you do build a custom control, add `.accessibilityLabel("...")` so that it is announced with a meaningful name. Test once by turning VoiceOver on in the Simulator or on a device, and listen to how your form sounds.
Animation

SwiftUI can animate almost any change in state. The simplest tool is `withAnimation`. Wrap the state change in it and every view that depends on that state moves smoothly to its new look. A second tool is the `.animation(_:value:)` modifier, which animates whenever one particular value changes.

items: `withAnimation { ... }` animates everything that changes because of the code inside.
A **transition** says how a view appears and disappears, as in `.transition(.opacity)`.
`.animation(_, value:)` animates only when `value` changes, which stops it from animating things you did not mean to.

Keep motion short and quiet. Very long or bouncy animations get in the way. Many people turn on *Reduce Motion* in their phone settings, and a careful app respects it. You can read it from the environment with `accessibilityReduceMotion`.

content.text: Spring animations and many animation names have changed between iOS versions. If a name does not compile for your minimum iOS version, use `.easeInOut`, which works everywhere.
Your task

items: Replace the add sheet with `ExpenseFormView`.
Show the error messages only after the first tap on Save, and clear them when the input is fixed.
Add a `ExpandableNote`-style details area in the detail screen that opens with an animation.
Turn on Reduce Motion in the Simulator's Accessibility settings and see how your app behaves.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: An empty title or a zero amount shows an error and does not save.
Choosing a category and a date saves them with the expense.
The expandable area opens and closes smoothly.

steps.say: The user fills in the form: title, amount, category and date.
When they tap Save, small computed properties check the input.
If something is wrong, a clear message appears next to that field and nothing is saved.
If everything is fine, the expense is saved and the sheet closes.

faqs.q: What is the difference between withAnimation and the animation modifier?
faqs.a: withAnimation wraps a state change and animates everything affected by it. The animation(_:value:) modifier animates a view only when one particular value changes.

faqs.q: How do I validate a form in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: Write the rules as small computed properties, check them in a save function, show errors next to the fields, and repeat the checks where the data is stored.

faqs.q: Why use CaseIterable with a Picker?
faqs.a: CaseIterable gives allCases, a list of every enum case, so ForEach can build all the picker choices without you typing them again.

quiz.q: What does withAnimation do?
options: Animates the views that change because of the state change inside it

quiz.q: Where should the rules for a valid form be checked?
options: On the screen and again where the data is saved

quiz.q: Why use CaseIterable on an enum with a Picker?
options: allCases lets ForEach build every choice
It makes the enum a class
It saves the enum to disk

notes: `Form` and `Section` give the grouped settings look. `Picker`, `DatePicker`, `TextField(value:format:)`.
Picker: bind the selection, give each choice a `.tag`. Enum + CaseIterable builds the list.
Validation in small computed properties. Show errors next to the field, after the first Save tap.
Check the rules again where data is saved, not only on screen.
`withAnimation { state.toggle() }` animates the change. `.animation(_, value:)` animates one value.
Keep motion short. Respect Reduce Motion. Give custom controls an accessibility label.

lessons.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await, Task, Actors and @MainActor
lessons.description: Learn why apps must not block the main thread, how async and await work, how to start work with Task and the task modifier, and what actors and @MainActor do.

content.text: An iPhone app has one special thread, the **main thread**, which draws the screen and handles taps. If you do slow work on it, such as waiting for a web server, the app freezes and the user thinks it has crashed. Apps must do slow work *off to the side* and come back to the main thread when the result is ready. Swift has a modern, readable way to write this, called **Swift Concurrency**. You will use it for networking in lesson 11 and for saving data after that.
Before async/await

In older code, slow work took a **completion handler**, a closure called later. Several in a row became a pyramid of nested braces that was hard to read and easy to get wrong. `async` and `await` let you write the same steps as ordinary code that reads from top to bottom.
async and await

items: A function marked **`async`** may need to wait. While it waits, the thread is free to do other work.
You call it with **`await`**. The word marks a *possible pause*. Your code stops at that line, and continues when the answer is ready. Meanwhile, the screen keeps working.
A function that is `async throws` combines this with lesson 5. You call it with `try await`.

content.text: `Task.sleep` is a stand-in for a real wait. In lesson 11 it becomes a real network call. The shape of the code stays the same, so learning it now with a fake delay is useful.
Starting async work: the task modifier and Task

You cannot call an `async` function from ordinary code, because ordinary code cannot pause. You start a new **task** instead. In SwiftUI the best way for work that belongs to a screen is the `.task` modifier. It starts when the view appears and is cancelled automatically when the view goes away.

This is the pattern behind most screens in real apps: show a spinner, wait for the data, then show the result or a friendly error. Notice that the code reads in order, with no nested closures. When you want a task from a button tap or other ordinary code, use `Task { ... }`.
Doing several things at once
If two calls do not depend on each other, start them together with `async let`, then `await` both. The total time is about the time of the slowest one, not the sum.
For a variable number of calls, such as one per item in an array, Swift has **task groups**. They are an advanced topic. It is enough now to know that they exist.
Actors and the main actor

When many tasks run at once and touch the same data, two of them can change it at the same moment and corrupt it. This is a **data race**. Swift's answer is the **actor**. An actor is like a class that handles one request at a time, so its data is safe. You call into an actor with `await`, because you may have to wait your turn.

The **main actor**, written `@MainActor`, is a special actor that stands for the main thread. Code that changes the screen has to run there. Views and anything they own are on the main actor already. When you write your own class that drives a screen, as in lesson 13, mark it `@MainActor` so the compiler checks this for you.

Swift 6 added stricter checks for data races, and newer Xcode versions can turn them on or run the main actor by default in new projects. You may see warnings that mention `Sendable`, which marks types that are safe to pass between tasks. Plain structs of simple values are usually fine. Read the message, and fix the one thing it names. Settings differ between Xcode versions, so check Apple's current notes if your project shows many.
Common mistakes

items: Doing slow work without `async`, which freezes the screen.
Changing the screen from the wrong thread. Mark view-driving classes `@MainActor`.
Starting a `Task` in `onAppear` that never stops. Prefer `.task`, which cancels itself.
Forgetting that after an `await`, other things may have changed. Do not assume the screen is as you left it.

content.text: Your task

Make `loadExpenses` throw an error on purpose and check that your message shows.
Add a Refresh button that uses `Task { ... }`.
Write the `ExpenseCache` actor and call it from a `Task`. Notice why `await` is needed.
