items: The list appears about a second after the screen opens, and the screen does not freeze meanwhile.
When you force an error, the red message shows and the spinner stops.
You can say what `await` marks and why an actor needs it.

steps.say: The main thread draws the screen and must never be blocked for long.
Slow work starts in a task, with the task modifier or Task.
At an await, the task pauses and the main thread keeps the screen alive.
When the answer is ready, the code continues and the screen updates with the result.

faqs.q: What does await do in Swift?
faqs.a: It marks a point where the code may pause until an async function gives its answer. While it waits, the thread is free to do other work, so the screen does not freeze.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Task and the task modifier?
faqs.a: The task modifier starts when a view appears and is cancelled when it disappears, so it suits work that belongs to a screen. Task { } starts work from ordinary code such as a button tap.

faqs.q: What is an actor in Swift?
faqs.a: A type like a class that handles one request at a time, so its data cannot be changed by two tasks at once. You call into it with await.

quiz.q: What happens at an await?
options: The code may pause while the thread stays free for other work

quiz.q: Which modifier starts async work when a view appears and cancels it when the view goes away?
What does an actor protect?
options: Its data from being changed by two tasks at once

notes: Main thread draws the screen. Slow work on it freezes the app.
`async` function may wait. Call it with `await` (a possible pause). `async throws` needs `try await`.
`.task { }` on a view starts when it appears and cancels when it leaves. `Task { }` starts work from a button.
`async let a = ...` runs independent calls at the same time. Task groups: for a variable number of calls.
Actor = class that handles one request at a time, so data cannot be corrupted. Call it with `await`.
`@MainActor` = runs on the main thread. Mark classes that drive the screen.

lessons.title: URLSession and Codable: Call a REST API from SwiftUI
lessons.metaTitle: URLSession and Codable: Call a REST API
lessons.description: Learn how to read JSON with Codable, call a web API with URLSession and async/await, handle bad responses, and show loading, result and error states in SwiftUI.

content.text: Most apps talk to a server. A weather app asks for the forecast, a shop app asks for products, a chat app sends your message to a language model. They all do it the same way: send an HTTP request, get back **JSON**, and turn the JSON into Swift values. In this lesson you build a small weather screen with the two tools Apple gives you for that, `URLSession` and `Codable`.
JSON and Codable

JSON is a plain-text format of keys and values. `Codable` is a Swift protocol (in fact a pair, `Encodable` and `Decodable`) that lets a struct turn into JSON and back, with almost no code. If the property names match the keys in the JSON, you are done. If they do not, you describe the difference with `CodingKeys`.

The three quote marks make a **multi-line string**. `Data(json.utf8)` turns text into the raw bytes that the decoder reads. Decoding can fail, for example if a key is missing or has the wrong type, so it is called with `try`. Fail-with-a-message is much better than a crash, so always keep it inside `do` and `catch`, or in a function that `throws`.

items: Nested JSON objects become nested structs, as above.
Keys that may be missing become optional properties, such as `let note: String?`.
Dates need a decoder setting, such as `decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601`.

For snake_case keys such as `first_name`, you can set `decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` instead of writing CodingKeys by hand. Names with digits, like `temperature_2m`, are better with explicit `CodingKeys`.

content.text: Calling the API with URLSession

`URLSession` is Apple's tool for network requests. Since Swift Concurrency arrived, the call is a single `await`. We use **Open-Meteo**, a weather service that was free to use for non-commercial projects without a key when this lesson was written. Check its current terms on its website before you use it in anything you publish.

We wrote the field names above from our reading of the service's documentation and could not run the call in the environment where this course was written. So do one thing first: paste the web address below into a browser and look at the real JSON. If the field names differ from the struct, change the `CodingKeys` to match. Reading a real response before writing a model is a good habit in any case.

items: `URLComponents` builds a web address safely, including the question mark and the encoding of special characters. It is better than gluing strings together.
`URLSession.shared.data(from:)` is `async throws`. It returns the bytes and a response object.
A server can answer with a failure code, for example 404 or 500, and `data(from:)` does not throw for it. You must check the status code yourself. Codes from 200 to 299 mean success.
Everything that can go wrong, no internet, a bad status, unexpected JSON, ends up as a thrown error that the screen can catch.

content.text: Showing loading, result and error
A network call has three outcomes the person needs to see: waiting, success and failure. An enum from lesson 4 models this nicely. The screen is then a simple `switch`.

The numbers 52.52 and 13.41 are the position of a city. Later you can ask for the user's location with Core Location, or let them type a city. The message in the `failed` case is written for a person. Do not show raw error text to users. It means nothing to them, and it can reveal things you would rather keep private.
Rules for real apps

items: **Use HTTPS.** iOS blocks plain `http` addresses by default for good reasons.

**Never put a secret key in the app.** Anything inside an app can be extracted. If an API needs a private key, such as a language model service, call your own server, which keeps the key and talks to the service for you. This is the pattern behind the AI courses on this site.
**Be ready for failure.** Phones lose signal, tunnels exist. Always have an error state and a retry.
**Do not call on every key press.** For search boxes, wait until the user stops typing for a moment.
**Respect the service's terms and rate limits.** Free services often have limits.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Assuming a 404 or 500 throws an error. You have to check the status code.
A struct that does not match the JSON, which gives a decoding error. Read the real response first.
Updating the screen from a background thread. In SwiftUI with `@State` and `.task`, you are on the main actor, which is what you want.

content.text: Your task

items: Decode the sample JSON in a Playground and print the temperature.
Open the Open-Meteo address in a browser, compare the real field names with your struct, and fix `CodingKeys` if needed.
Build `WeatherView` and run it. Turn on Airplane Mode in the Simulator's host settings or use a wrong address to see the error state and the retry button.
Add a `TextField` for a city and one more field, such as a time or a unit, decoded from the response.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The screen shows a spinner, then a temperature, and a retry button when the call fails.
You can say why a 404 does not throw by itself.
You can say why a secret API key must never be inside the app.

steps.say: The screen starts a task and shows a spinner while it waits.
URLSession sends an HTTPS request to the web address.
The server answers with a status code and JSON. You must check the status yourself.
JSONDecoder turns the JSON into your Codable struct, and the screen shows the result or an error.

faqs.q: What is Codable in Swift?
faqs.a: A protocol that lets a type be turned into and read from formats such as JSON. If property names match the keys, you write almost no code. CodingKeys handle differences.

faqs.q: Does URLSession throw an error for a 404 response?
faqs.a: No. It throws for problems such as no connection, but a 404 or 500 comes back as a normal response. Check the status code and throw your own error.

faqs.q: Is it safe to put an API key inside an iOS app?
faqs.a: No. Anything in an app can be extracted. Keep private keys on your own server and let the app call that server.

quiz.q: Does URLSession throw an error for a 404 response?
options: No, you must check the status code yourself

quiz.q: What is Codable used for?
options: Turning a struct into JSON and back

quiz.q: Where should a private API key be kept?
options: On your own server, not inside the app
quiz.explain: Anything inside an app can be extracted.

notes: Codable = struct to JSON and back. `CodingKeys` map different key names.
Decoding can fail. Use `try` inside `do` and `catch`.
`try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)`. A 404 or 500 does NOT throw. Check the status (200 to 299 is success).
`URLComponents` builds a safe address. Use HTTPS only.
Show three states: loading, loaded, failed (with a retry). An enum plus `switch` models this.
Never put a private API key in the app. Call your own server. Read the real JSON before writing the model.

lessons.title: SwiftData: Save and Query Data on the iPhone
lessons.metaTitle: SwiftData: Save and Query Data on iPhone
lessons.description: Make the Expense Tracker remember its data with SwiftData: the Model macro, ModelContainer, Query, insert, delete, sorting, filtering and AppStorage.

content.text: Right now the Expense Tracker forgets everything when you close it. To keep data on the phone you need **persistence**. Apple's modern tool for it is **SwiftData**, which arrived with iOS 17. It sits on the same storage technology as the older **Core Data**, but it is written in plain Swift, and it works well with SwiftUI. You will still see Core Data and plain SQLite in jobs, so know that they exist. Start with SwiftData for new apps with a minimum of iOS 17.
Make the model storable

Change the `Expense` struct to a class and put `@Model` in front of it. This one macro makes the class storable and observable. A class is needed here because SwiftData tracks changes to one shared object, which is the case where lesson 4 said a class is the right choice.
Properties of simple types, text, numbers, dates, booleans and enums that are `Codable`, are stored automatically. You do not write a table, a schema or any SQL. The `id` is looked after for you.
Give the app a container
A **model container** is the database for your app. You attach it once, at the top, and every view below it can use it.
Read with @Query, write with modelContext

`@Query` loads stored objects into a property and keeps it up to date. When something is added or changed, the view redraws by itself, the same way as with `@State`. To change data you use the **model context**, which the system puts in the environment.

items: `@Query(sort:order:)` fetches and sorts. The path `\Expense.date` points to the property to sort by.

`modelContext.insert(_:)` stores a new object, and `modelContext.delete(_:)` removes one. SwiftData saves automatically at sensible moments, and you can call `try modelContext.save()` when you want to be sure.
Editing is simply changing a property of a stored object, for example `expense.title = "Dinner"`. SwiftData notices, and the screen updates.
`ContentUnavailableView` is the built-in empty state for a screen with nothing to show.

content.text: The form from lesson 9 already builds an `Expense` when the user taps Save and hands it back through `onSave`. Nothing is stored until we call `insert`, so cancelling leaves no half-finished object in the database. Two small changes are needed for the new model: `Expense` is now a class with the `init` shown above, and the `Category` enum must be `Codable`, as written in this lesson. Remove the older `Category` and `Expense` definitions from lesson 8 so the names are not defined twice.
Filtering

A **predicate** says which objects to load. It is written in normal-looking Swift with the `#Predicate` macro. Because the filter value often comes from outside the view, the usual trick is to set the query in the view's `init`.
Previews and testing with a temporary database
In previews and tests you do not want to touch real data. Make a container that lives only in memory.
Small settings: AppStorage
For a single setting, such as a currency code or a dark mode choice, a database is too much. `@AppStorage` keeps a small value in the app's user defaults and acts like `@State`.
@AppStorage("currencyCode") private var currencyCode = "USD"
Things to know before you ship

items: **Changing the model later** needs care. Adding a property with a default is usually easy. Renaming or removing one needs a *migration*. While you are learning, deleting the app from the Simulator starts you fresh. Before real users have data, read Apple's notes on schema versions.
**Money** should use `Decimal` in a real finance app, because `Double` cannot hold some decimal values exactly. We kept `Double` to keep the lessons short.

**Sync across devices** is possible with iCloud, but it needs extra set-up in your developer account, and we do not cover it here. Services such as Firebase are another route, and many job posts mention them. Learn them after the basics.
**Core Data** is older and still everywhere in existing apps. Its ideas, a container, a context, fetch requests and saving, map directly to what you just learned.

content.text: Your task

items: Change `Expense` to a `@Model` class and add the model container to the app.
Replace the in-memory array with `@Query`, and make add and swipe to delete work with `modelContext`.
Close the app completely in the Simulator, open it again, and check that the data is still there.
Add a screen that shows only expenses above an amount typed in a field, using `#Predicate`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your expenses are still there after you restart the app.
The newest expense is at the top.
You can say the difference between `@State`, `@Query` and `@AppStorage`.

steps.say: The user adds an expense in the form.
Your code inserts a new object into the model context.
The context saves it into the container, which keeps it on the phone.
The query reads the stored data back, and the list redraws with the new row.

faqs.q: What is SwiftData?
faqs.a: Apple's modern framework for saving data on the device, written in Swift and designed to work with SwiftUI. It needs iOS 17 or newer and builds on the same storage as Core Data.

faqs.q: Should I learn Core Data or SwiftData?
faqs.a: Start with SwiftData for new apps. Core Data is older and still found in many existing apps, and its ideas of container, context and saving are the same.

faqs.q: Why does my data disappear in previews?
faqs.a: Previews often use an in-memory container, so nothing is kept. That is intended. Run the app in the Simulator to test real saving.

quiz.q: Which macro makes a class storable with SwiftData?
How do you read stored objects into a SwiftUI view?
What is the best tool for one small setting such as a currency code?

notes: SwiftData needs iOS 17+. `@Model final class Expense` makes it storable.
`.modelContainer(for: Expense.self)` on the app's scene = the database.
`@Query(sort:order:)` loads objects and the view updates by itself.
`@Environment(\.modelContext)`: `insert(obj)`, `delete(obj)`, `save()`. Editing a property is enough to update.
`#Predicate` filters. Previews: `inMemory: true`.
`@AppStorage("key")` for small settings. Changing the model later may need a migration. Money: use `Decimal` in real apps.

lessons.title: MVVM in SwiftUI: @Observable, Dependency Injection and Clean Code
lessons.description: Move logic out of views with MVVM, use the Observable macro, inject services through protocols, and meet MVC, VIPER, Clean Architecture and Repository.

content.text: As an app grows, views fill up with logic: validation, network calls, sorting rules. They become hard to read and impossible to test without a screen. **Architecture** is the set of habits that keeps each piece of code in a sensible place. Interviewers ask about it a lot, and teams use it to keep big apps maintainable. This lesson explains the pattern most SwiftUI teams use, **MVVM**, and then walks through the others you will hear about.
MVVM in one picture

items: **Model**: the data and its rules. Your structs and `@Model` classes, such as `Expense`.
**View**: what the user sees. A SwiftUI struct that shows data and sends user actions.
**ViewModel**: a class in the middle. It holds the state the view needs, and does the work: loads from the network, validates, sorts, and decides what to show.

content.text: The view *reads* the view model and *tells* it what the user did. The view model knows nothing about SwiftUI controls. That makes it easy to test, because a test can create a view model and call its methods with no screen at all.
@Observable

In iOS 17 Apple added the `@Observable` macro. Put it on a class, and SwiftUI watches the properties that a view actually reads. When one of them changes, only the views that used it are redrawn. Before this, you used `ObservableObject` with `@Published` properties and `@StateObject`. You will see that style in older tutorials and code bases, and it relates to the **Combine** framework, Apple's older tool for streams of values over time. New code on iOS 17 and up does not need either of them for this job.

`@MainActor` from lesson 10 makes sure this class changes the screen's data on the main thread. `private(set)` means the view can read `state` but only the view model can change it. And the `service` arrives through the `init`, which brings us to the second big idea.
Dependency injection

**Dependency injection** sounds grand and means something simple: *a type receives the things it needs from outside, and does not create them itself.* The view model above does not write `WeatherService()` inside. It asks for something that can fetch weather. We describe that ability with a protocol, from lesson 4.

Now the view model works with any type that meets the protocol. In the real app you give it the real service. In a preview you give it a fake one that answers at once with sample data, with no internet. In a test you give it a fake that fails on purpose, to check your error handling. This is the main practical reason for the whole idea.
Using the view model in a view

If Xcode complains about main-actor isolation in the view's `init` (newer Xcode versions are stricter), mark the view's `init` or the whole view `@MainActor`. The message names the line, and the fix is one word.

With an `@Observable` class, the view keeps it in `@State`, so that SwiftUI creates it once and keeps it alive. For something shared by many screens, such as the logged-in user or app settings, you can put the object in the **environment** with `.environment(settings)` at the top, and read it in any view with `@Environment(Settings.self)`.
The other names you will hear

items: **MVC** (Model View Controller): Apple's original pattern for UIKit. The view controller often grew huge, which gave rise to the joke name *Massive View Controller*. MVVM was partly a reaction to it.
**VIPER** (View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity, Router): splits an app into many small pieces with strict roles. It brings a lot of files, so you see it in some large UIKit teams.
**Clean Architecture**: arranges code in layers, so that business rules do not depend on screens, databases or the network.
**Coordinator pattern**: one object decides which screen comes next, so that screens do not know about each other. Popular in UIKit. SwiftUI's `NavigationStack` covers much of this need.

**Repository pattern**: one type is the single place to get and save a kind of data. The view model asks the repository, and does not care whether the data comes from the network, a file or the database.
**SOLID**: five design habits, such as *one reason to change per type* and *depend on protocols, not on concrete types*. What you did with `WeatherServing` is one of them.

content.text: Do not over-build. A small app with a few screens does not need five layers. For simple screens, `@Query` straight in a view is fine, and Apple's own examples do it. Add a view model when a screen has real logic or needs tests. The skill that interviewers look for is knowing *why* you choose a structure, and not how many layers you can draw.
Common mistakes

items: Creating the service inside the view model, which makes tests need the real network.
Passing the whole view model to every small child view. Pass just the values and closures the child needs.
Making a view model that imports SwiftUI types, such as `Color`, which ties logic to the screen.

content.text: Your task

items: Move the networking logic of `WeatherView` into `WeatherViewModel`.
Add the `WeatherServing` protocol and a `FakeWeatherService`.
Use the fake in a `#Preview` so that it shows a temperature with no internet.
Write down, in your own words, three things MVVM gives you and one case where it would be too much.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The app works as before, and the preview works without a network.
The view does not contain any call to `URLSession`.
You can explain dependency injection in one sentence, with the weather example.

steps.say: The view shows the state and tells the view model what the user did.
The view model holds the state and the logic, with no SwiftUI controls inside.
It talks to its service only through a protocol, so it does not know which one it has.
The app gives it the real service. Previews and tests give it a fake one.

faqs.q: What is MVVM in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: A way to split an app: the model holds data and rules, the view shows it, and the view model sits between them with the state and logic. It makes logic easy to test without a screen.

faqs.q: What is the difference between @Observable and ObservableObject?
faqs.a: @Observable is the newer macro for iOS 17 and up. Views redraw only for the properties they read. ObservableObject with @Published is the older approach that you will still see in many code bases.

faqs.q: What is dependency injection?
faqs.a: A type receives what it needs from outside instead of creating it. With a protocol, you can inject a real service in the app and a fake one in previews and tests.

quiz.q: In MVVM, what does the view model hold?
options: The state and logic the view needs

quiz.q: What is dependency injection?
options: A type receives what it needs from outside instead of creating it
quiz.explain: With a protocol you can inject a fake in tests and previews.

quiz.q: Which macro, for iOS 17 and up, makes a class observable by SwiftUI views?

notes: MVVM: Model = data, View = screen, ViewModel = state and logic between them.
`@Observable` class (iOS 17+) replaces ObservableObject/@Published. Views redraw only for properties they read.
Mark view models `@MainActor`. `private(set)` lets only the view model change state.
Dependency injection: pass in what a type needs (a protocol), do not create it inside.
Real service in the app, fake in previews and tests.
MVC, VIPER, Clean Architecture, Coordinator, Repository, SOLID: know the names. Do not over-build small apps.

lessons.title: Testing iOS Apps: Swift Testing, XCTest and XCUITest
lessons.metaTitle: Testing iOS Apps: Swift Testing and XCTest
lessons.description: Write unit tests with Swift Testing and XCTest, test a view model with a fake service, automate taps with XCUITest, and learn what Quick and Nimble are.

content.text: A test is a small program that runs your code and checks the result. You write it once, and it checks again every time you change something. Tests do not remove all bugs. They catch the ones that would come back, and they let you change code without fear. Employers value them because they show you can work on code other people depend on.
What kinds of tests there are

items: **Unit tests** check a small piece of logic, such as a validation rule or a view model, with no screen.
**UI tests** drive the real app like a user: launch, tap, type and look at what appears. They are slower, so write fewer of them for the main flows.
**Manual testing** still matters, on real phones, with different text sizes and with no network.

content.text: In Xcode, tick **Include Tests** when you create a project, or add a **Unit Testing Bundle** target to an existing one. You run tests with Command and U, or with the small diamond next to a test. A green mark means it passed.
Swift Testing

**Swift Testing** is Apple's newer test framework, available from Xcode 16. A test is a function with `@Test`. You check values with `#expect`. If an expectation is false, the test fails and the message shows both sides.

items: `@testable import` lets tests see your app's internal code. Use your own app's module name.
`#expect(throws:)` checks that a call throws the error you expect.
`@Test(arguments:)` runs the same test once for each value, which keeps the list of cases in one place.
A test that throws is a failed test, so mark such tests `throws`.

content.text: Testing a view model with a fake
This is where the work of lesson 13 pays off. We give the view model a fake service that fails, and check that the state becomes `failed`.
The test never touches the internet, so it is fast and always gives the same result. That is what you want from a unit test. `Issue.record` fails the test with a message of your choice.
XCTest

**XCTest** is the older framework, and it is still everywhere. Test classes inherit from `XCTestCase`, and every method whose name starts with `test` runs. You check values with functions such as `XCTAssertEqual`. UI tests use XCTest too. Expect to read both styles in jobs, and the same ideas apply.
Comparing decimal numbers needs an *accuracy* value, as above, because decimal arithmetic on computers is not always exact. The same is true in many languages.
XCUITest: testing like a user

Add a **UI Testing Bundle** target. A UI test launches your app in a separate process and finds controls by their label or by an **accessibility identifier**, a name you give to a view so tests, and assistive tools, can find it.

UI tests can be slow and a little fragile, so keep them for your most important paths, such as signing in or adding the main item. For these tests you often want a clean, known state, for example an in-memory database from lesson 12 and a fake service. A common trick is to pass a launch argument that tells the app to use them.
Quick and Nimble, and what to do first

**Quick** and **Nimble** are third-party libraries that offer a more descriptive style of test, `describe` and `it`, which some teams like. You do not need them. Learn Swift Testing and XCTest first, because they come from Apple and every project can use them.
A sensible testing habit

items: Test logic that could go wrong: validation, calculations, view models, parsing JSON.
Do not test that SwiftUI draws a `Text`. That is Apple's job.
Name tests as sentences, such as `rejectsEmptyTitle`. A failure then explains itself.
When you find a bug, write a failing test first, fix the code, and keep the test.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a test target if your project has none. Write the three validation tests above.
Write a test that checks the total of three expenses.
Write the failing-service test for your view model.
Write one UI test that adds an expense. Give the button and fields accessibility identifiers.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All tests pass with Command and U. Change an expected value on purpose and see one fail with a clear message.
No unit test uses the real network.
You can say when to write a unit test and when a UI test.

steps.say: A test creates your code, such as a view model, with the inputs you choose.
It hands the code a fake service, so nothing real is called and the result is always the same.
The test runs one action and compares the result with what you expect.
Xcode shows green when it matches and a clear message when it does not.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Swift Testing and XCTest?
faqs.a: Swift Testing is Apple's newer framework from Xcode 16, using @Test and #expect. XCTest is the older one with XCTestCase and XCTAssert functions. Both are in use, and UI tests still use XCTest.

faqs.q: What should I unit test in an iOS app?
faqs.a: Logic that can go wrong: validation, calculations, view models and JSON parsing. Do not test that SwiftUI draws basic views.

faqs.q: Why use an accessibility identifier?
faqs.a: It gives a view a stable name so UI tests, and assistive tools, can find it, even if its visible text changes or is translated.

quiz.q: Which Swift Testing macro marks a test function?
Why give a view model a fake service in a unit test?
options: The test is fast and gives the same result every time

quiz.q: What helps a UI test find a button reliably?

notes: Unit test = small check of logic. UI test = drives the real app. Run all with Cmd+U.
Swift Testing (Xcode 16+): `@Test`, `#expect`, `#expect(throws:)`, `@Test(arguments:)`.
XCTest (older, still everywhere): `XCTestCase`, `testSomething()`, `XCTAssertEqual`.
Fake service in a unit test = fast, no network, same result every time.
XCUITest: `XCUIApplication()`, `.launch()`, `app.buttons["id"].tap()`. Give views `.accessibilityIdentifier`.
Test logic that can go wrong. Do not test that SwiftUI draws a Text.

lessons.title: Project 2: Calculator App with an Expression Parser
lessons.description: Build a calculator in Swift and SwiftUI with its own expression parser, correct order of operations, error handling, a keypad grid and Swift Testing unit tests.

content.text: A calculator looks like the easiest app there is, which makes it a good first project after the Expense Tracker. The screen is simple, but the logic is real: you must turn the text "2+3*4" into 14, not 20. Many beginners reach for a library. Here you write a small parser yourself, so you learn how text becomes a result, and you keep it in a plain Swift type that you can test without launching the Simulator.

The screen is a grid of buttons, a display for the expression and a line for the result or an error. The state lives in an @Observable model, the same pattern as lesson 13, so the view only describes what to show.
Concepts in this project

items: **Tokenising**: splitting "12+3.5*2" into numbers and operators. A minus at the very start belongs to the first number.
**Order of operations**: pass one handles * and /, pass two handles + and -. This matches mathematics.
**Failing safely**: `evaluate` returns an optional. A nil means invalid input, and the screen shows a message instead of crashing.
**Separating logic from UI**: `Calculator` is an enum with static functions and no SwiftUI import, so tests call it directly.
**Button grids**: `ForEach` over rows of labels, `frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` so keys share the width.
**Swift Testing**: `@Test` functions with `#expect`, one small fact per test.

content.text: Create the project

The code
**`Calculator.swift`**

Walkthrough

Start with `tokens`. It walks through the text one character at a time and builds a number in a string called `current`. When it meets an operator it converts that string to a Double, stores it, then stores the operator. Spaces are skipped, and any other character makes the function return nil, so letters cannot get through. The special case is the minus sign: when `current` is empty and nothing has been stored yet, the minus is the start of a negative number, so it becomes the first character of `current`.

`evaluate` then reads the tokens in pairs: an operator followed by a number. For * and / it changes the last number in the list straight away, which is how multiplication gets done before addition. For + and - it saves the operator and the next number for the second pass. Division by zero returns nil. The second pass is a plain loop that adds or subtracts from left to right.

`CalculatorModel` is tiny on purpose. `press` handles five kinds of key: clear, backspace, equals, and everything else, which is appended to the expression. After a successful equals the expression becomes the result, so you can keep calculating. The model never draws anything, so you could reuse it in a Mac or watch app.

In the view, `rows` is an array of arrays of strings. Two nested ForEach loops build the grid. `id: \.self` is fine here because every label is unique. The colour function gives operators orange and the clear keys grey, which is a small touch that makes the keypad easier to read.

items: A key calls `model.press(key)`. The model changes `expression` or `result`, and SwiftUI redraws because the model is @Observable.
`evaluate` tokenises, runs the multiplication and division pass, then the addition and subtraction pass.
Any unexpected input returns nil, and the model sets `hasError` so the result line turns red.
`format` prints 14.0 as 14 and keeps 3.75 as it is.

lessons.title: Project 3: To-Do App with SwiftData, Filters and Tests
lessons.description: Build a to-do app with SwiftData that saves tasks on the iPhone: a @Query list, swipe to delete, a segmented filter and tests with an in-memory store.

content.text: A to-do list is the standard first app with a database, because it needs the four basic operations: create, read, update and delete. SwiftData makes this short. You mark a class with @Model, give the app a model container, and a @Query in the view always shows the current rows. When a task changes, the screen changes, and when the app is closed the tasks stay.
This project also shows how to test SwiftData without touching real data. A test creates a container that lives only in memory, so each test starts empty and leaves nothing behind.
Concepts in this project

items: **@Model**: turns a class into a stored type. Plain properties become saved columns.
**modelContainer(for:)**: set once on the scene. It creates the store and gives every view a model context.
**@Query**: a property wrapper that fetches and keeps the list updated, with sorting built in.
**Insert, change, delete**: `context.insert`, setting a property such as `isDone`, and `context.delete`. SwiftData saves automatically.
**A filter enum**: `TodoFilter.apply(to:)` keeps the filtering rule in one testable place.
**In-memory test store**: `ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true)`.

The code
**`TodoItem.swift`**
**`TodoListView.swift`**
**`TodoApp.swift`**
**`TodoTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`TodoItem` is a final class with three properties. The initialiser gives `isDone` and `createdAt` default values, so creating a task needs only a title. `@Model` is a macro, so you do not write any storage code yourself.

In `TodoListView`, `@Environment(\.modelContext)` gives the view the context it uses to insert and delete. `@Query(sort: \TodoItem.createdAt, order: .reverse)` returns the newest tasks first. Because the wrapper observes the store, you never refresh the list by hand.

The `add` function trims spaces, ignores empty titles, inserts a new item and clears the text field. The same function is used by the Add button and by pressing return, through `onSubmit`. Reusing one function keeps both paths identical.

Delete needs care. Swipe-to-delete gives you positions in the list that is shown, which may be filtered, not positions in the full list. So `delete(at:)` applies the filter again and deletes the items at those positions in the filtered list. Using the unfiltered list here would delete the wrong task, which is a classic bug.

The tests build a container with `isStoredInMemoryOnly: true`, save two items and fetch them back. The second test checks the filter without a database at all, because `TodoFilter.apply` is a plain function over an array.
How it works

items: The scene's `modelContainer(for: TodoItem.self)` creates the store and shares a context with every view.
`@Query` fetches the items sorted by date, and redraws the list whenever they change.
Tapping a row toggles `isDone`. Because the item is a model object, the change is saved.
The segmented picker changes `filter`, and the list shows `filter.apply(to: items)`.

Tap it: the circle fills and the text is crossed out. Choose Open: it disappears from the list. Swipe a row left and delete it. Quit the app from the app switcher and open it again: the remaining tasks are still there. Both tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 4: Habit Tracker with Streaks and Date Logic
lessons.description: Build a habit tracker in SwiftUI that counts daily streaks, saves habits as JSON in UserDefaults, handles dates safely with Calendar and tests the streak rules.

content.text: Habit apps look simple, but they teach one of the hardest parts of real software: dates. What is "today"? What is "yesterday" when the phone changes time zone? This project keeps the rules small and testable. Each day a habit is done is stored as a text key such as "2026-11-10", and the streak is the number of days in a row counted back from today.

Storage is deliberately plain. The habits are encoded as JSON and saved in UserDefaults, which is enough for a small list and shows you how Codable works on its own. For larger data, use SwiftData, as in the previous project.
Concepts in this project

items: **Codable structs**: `Habit` becomes JSON with `JSONEncoder` and back with `JSONDecoder`.
**Day keys**: a text such as 2026-11-10 avoids time-of-day and time zone surprises in sets and comparisons.
**Calendar arithmetic**: `calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -1, to:)` instead of subtracting 86,400 seconds, which breaks on daylight saving days.
**Streak rule**: count back from today. If today is not done yet, start from yesterday so the streak is not lost before the day ends.
**Injected dependencies**: the functions take `today` and `calendar` parameters, so tests can use a fixed date and a fixed time zone.
**didSet persistence**: the store saves whenever `habits` changes.

items: In Xcode choose File > New > Project > iOS > App. Set Interface to SwiftUI, Language to Swift, and Testing System to Swift Testing. Set the minimum deployment to iOS 17, because the code uses @Observable. Name the product Habits.

Habits/
  HabitApp.swift     @main
  Habit.swift        model, DayKey, streak rule
  HabitStore.swift   @Observable store saved as JSON
  HabitView.swift    list, add, tick today
HabitsTests/
  HabitTests.swift
The code
**`Habit.swift`**
**`HabitStore.swift`**
**`HabitView.swift`**
**`HabitApp.swift`**
**`HabitTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`Habit` stores its completed days in a `Set<String>`. A set gives fast lookups and cannot hold the same day twice. `DayKey.key(for:)` builds the text from the year, month and day parts of a date. Because it uses only those three parts, two moments on the same calendar day produce the same key.

The streak function is the heart of the project. It first checks whether today is done. If not, it moves to yesterday, so a streak of 5 stays 5 until midnight passes without a tick. Then a loop counts days while each one is in the set, moving one day back each time. The loop stops at the first gap.

Notice the default parameters `today: Date = .now` and `calendar: Calendar = .current`. In the app you never pass them. In tests you pass a fixed calendar in UTC and fixed dates, so the result is the same on every machine and in every time zone. This is the standard way to make time-dependent code testable.

`HabitStore` loads in its initialiser and saves in `didSet`. `didSet` does not run during initialisation, which avoids saving the same data right after loading it. `toggleToday` finds the habit by id, then inserts or removes today's key. The view reads `habit.isDone(on: .now)` to choose the filled or empty circle.

The tests cover the main rules: three days in a row, a streak that survives until today is done, a gap that breaks the streak, no days at all, and the padded key format. Five small tests like this catch almost every date bug before a user does.
How it works

items: The view shows each habit with its streak and a circle button for today.
Tapping the circle calls `toggleToday`, which edits the set of day keys.
`didSet` on `habits` encodes the list to JSON and writes it to UserDefaults.
On the next launch the store decodes the JSON and the habits come back.

content.text: Expected output

The screen shows a text box with an Add button and the message "No habits yet." Add "Read 10 pages": it appears with "Streak: 0 day(s)". Tap the circle: it fills and the streak shows 1. Tap again: it empties and the streak returns to 0. Close and reopen the app: the habit is still there. Swipe to delete a habit. The five tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 5: Quiz App with Game State and Tests
lessons.description: Build a quiz app in SwiftUI with instant feedback, a score, a progress bar and a shuffled restart, using an @Observable engine and Swift Testing.

content.text: A quiz is a small state machine. At any moment the app is showing one question, waiting for an answer, showing feedback, or showing the final score. If you write the rules in one place, the screen becomes easy. If you scatter them across buttons, you get bugs such as scoring twice when a user taps fast. This project puts every rule in a `QuizEngine` class and keeps the view free of logic.
Because the engine is a plain @Observable class with no UI code, the tests can play a full game in a few lines. This is the same separation you used for the calculator, applied to a game.
Concepts in this project

items: **A state machine**: current question, selected answer, score and finished are enough to describe the whole game.
**private(set)**: the view can read `score` and `index` but only the engine can change them.
**Guarding rules**: `choose` ignores a second tap, and `next` does nothing before an answer.
**Feedback colours**: green for the right answer, red for the chosen wrong answer, grey for the rest.
**ProgressView**: shows how far through the quiz the user is.
**Shuffling on restart**: `questions.shuffle()` gives a new order each time.

**`Question.swift`**

import Foundation

struct Question: Identifiable, Equatable {
    let id = UUID()
    let text: String
    let options: [String]
    let answerIndex: Int
    let explanation: String
}

enum SampleQuestions {

                 options: ["let", "var", "const"],
                 answerIndex: 0,
                 explanation: "let makes a value that cannot be reassigned. var makes one that can."),
        Question(text: "What does an optional such as String? hold?",
                 options: ["A String or nil", "Always a String", "Only numbers"],
                 answerIndex: 0,
                 explanation: "An optional is either a value or nil, and Swift makes you handle both."),
        Question(text: "Which property wrapper stores state owned by a SwiftUI view?",
                 options: ["@State", "@Published", "@Model"],
                 answerIndex: 0,
                 explanation: "@State keeps a value that the view owns and redraws when it changes."),
        Question(text: "What is the difference between a struct and a class?",
                 options: ["Structs are copied, classes are shared", "Structs cannot have functions", "There is none"],
                 answerIndex: 0,
                 explanation: "Structs are value types and are copied. Classes are reference types and are shared."),
        Question(text: "Which call starts an async function?",
                 options: ["await", "async let only", "defer"],
                 answerIndex: 0,
                 explanation: "You call an async function with await, inside an async context such as a Task.")
    ]
}
**`QuizEngine.swift`**
**`QuizView.swift`**
**`QuizApp.swift`**
**`QuizTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`Question` holds the text, the options, the index of the right option and a short explanation. Storing the answer as an index keeps the data small. The sample questions are plain Swift code, so you can see the shape of the data and replace it with your own or load it from JSON later.

`QuizEngine` marks its properties `private(set)`. That is a useful habit: the view can show the score but cannot change it, so every change goes through `choose`, `next` or `restart`. In `choose`, the first guard returns if there is no current question or if an answer is already selected. That single line is what prevents double scoring.

`next` also begins with a guard. Without a selected answer it does nothing, so the Next button cannot skip a question even if the view has a bug. This is defensive design: the engine protects its own rules instead of trusting the screen.

The view uses an optional: `if let question = engine.current`. When the quiz is over, `current` is nil and the finished screen appears. This is a clean way to model two screens from one piece of state. The option buttons are disabled after an answer, and their tint comes from one small function that looks at the selected and correct indexes.

The four tests describe the rules as sentences: a correct answer scores, a second tap is ignored, Next needs an answer, and the quiz finishes after the last question with the right score. If you ever change the engine, these tests tell you at once whether a rule broke.

items: The view asks the engine for `current`. If there is a question it draws it, otherwise it draws the result.
A tap calls `choose`. The engine records the answer and adds to the score if it is right.
The view sees `hasAnswered`, colours the buttons, shows the explanation and offers Next.
After the last question, `isFinished` becomes true and the score screen appears. Play again shuffles and resets.

lessons.title: Project 6: Recipe Book App with Search and an API
lessons.metaTitle: Project 6: Recipe Book with an API
lessons.description: Build a recipe app that searches the free TheMealDB API with a debounce, shows loading, empty and error states and uses AsyncImage and NavigationStack.

content.text: This project joins everything from the networking lesson: Codable models, an async service, a view model with clear states and a navigation list. The data comes from TheMealDB, a free recipe service with a public test key. The user types in a search box, the app waits a moment, and then it calls the service and shows the matching dishes. Tapping one opens the full instructions.

Two details make the app feel professional. The first is a short wait (a debounce) so the app does not send a request for every key press. The second is a screen for every state: nothing searched yet, loading, no results, an error and the list. Many beginner apps show only the happy path.
Concepts in this project

items: **Codable with CodingKeys**: the service names fields such as strMeal, and the model renames them to name.
**A null list**: the service answers `{"meals": null}` when nothing matches, so `meals` is optional.
**Protocol for the service**: `RecipeService` lets tests use a fake instead of the network.
**State enum**: idle, loading, loaded and failed make the screen simple to write.
**Debounce with Task**: cancel the old search task and start a new one after a 400 millisecond sleep.
**ContentUnavailableView**: ready-made empty and error screens in iOS 17.

content.text: Create the project

items: In Xcode choose File > New > Project > iOS > App. Set Interface to SwiftUI, Language to Swift, and Testing System to Swift Testing. Set the minimum deployment to iOS 17, because the code uses @Observable. Name the product RecipeBook.

RecipeBook/

  RecipeService.swift   protocol + MealDBService

The code
**`Recipe.swift`**
**`RecipeService.swift`**
**`RecipeViewModel.swift`**
**`RecipeViews.swift`**
**`RecipeApp.swift`**
**`RecipeTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`Recipe` uses `CodingKeys` to connect the service's field names to clean Swift names. Most fields are optional because the service does not always fill them. `RecipeResponse` wraps the top-level object, with `meals` as an optional array. Decoding the null case into nil, then using `?? []`, turns "no results" into an empty list.

`MealDBService` builds the address with `URLComponents` and `URLQueryItem`, which encodes the search text safely. Typing "mac & cheese" works because the ampersand is escaped for you. It then checks the status code before decoding, as in lesson 11.

The view model is marked `@MainActor`, so changes to `state` happen on the main thread. `queryChanged` is the debounce: it cancels the previous task, ignores searches shorter than two letters, and starts a new task that sleeps for 400 milliseconds. If the user types another letter during that time, this task is cancelled and never calls the service. `load` handles the call and catches errors into the failed state.

In the view, a `switch` on `model.state` chooses what to show. `searchable` adds the search field, and `onChange(of:)` calls `queryChanged`. `navigationDestination(for: Recipe.self)` connects a tapped row to the detail screen. `AsyncImage` loads the picture and shows a grey placeholder meanwhile.

The tests do not use the network. They decode sample JSON, including the null case, and run the view model with a fake service that returns either a recipe or an error. Tests that depend on a real server fail when the server is slow or offline, so they are worse than useless.
How it works

items: The user types. `onChange` calls `queryChanged`, which waits 400 milliseconds before searching.
`load` sets the loading state, calls the service and sets loaded or failed.
The view draws the right screen for each state.
Tapping a row pushes the detail view with the whole recipe.

On launch the screen says "Search for a dish". Type "chicken": a spinner shows briefly and then a list of dishes with small pictures, categories and countries appears. Type a nonsense word: "No Results for ..." appears. Tap a dish: a detail screen shows a large picture and the instructions. Turn on Airplane Mode and search again: the screen shows "Could not load recipes" with a message. The four tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 7: Shopping App with Products and a Cart
lessons.metaTitle: Project 7: Shopping App with a Cart
lessons.description: Build a shopping app with products from the Fake Store API, a product grid, a saved cart in exact cents, quantity steppers and a demo checkout.

content.text: Shopping apps are a favourite interview project because they combine a network list, images, shared state between two screens and exact money. This project builds the core of one. Products come from the Fake Store API, the cart is saved on the phone, and the checkout is a **demo** that empties the cart and takes no payment.

A real shop needs a sign-in, addresses, a server that creates orders, a payment provider and legal pages. The lesson points to where each of these would go, but it does not pretend that a demo is a finished shop. Never put card numbers into your own screens. Use Apple Pay or a payment provider's hosted checkout and confirm the order on your server.
Concepts in this project

items: **Exact money**: prices become whole cents the moment a product enters the cart, and totals are sums of integers.
**A shared store**: one `CartStore` object is passed to both tabs, so the badge, the list and the total always agree.
**Computed values**: `totalCents` and `itemCount` are calculated from the lines, so they cannot go out of date.
**TabView with a badge**: the Cart tab shows the number of items.
**LazyVGrid with adaptive columns**: the grid fits two columns on a phone and more on an iPad.
**Extension for formatting**: `Int.asMoney` turns 4990 into $49.90.

Walkthrough

`Product` mirrors the service's JSON, with the price as a Double because that is what the service sends. The computed property `priceCents` rounds `price * 100` to the nearest whole number. Rounding matters: 109.95 times 100 is not exactly 10995 in floating point, so you must round, not truncate. From that point on, the cart never touches a Double again.

`CartLine` stores the product id, title, price in cents and quantity. It copies the title and price at the time of adding, which is how real carts work: a later price change should not silently change an order already in progress. `lineTotalCents` multiplies price by quantity.

`CartStore` is an @Observable class. The `add` function either raises the quantity of an existing line or appends a new one. `change(_:by:)` adjusts a quantity and removes the line when it reaches zero. Every change to `lines` triggers `didSet`, which encodes the cart to JSON and saves it to UserDefaults, so the cart survives closing the app.

In `ShopRootView`, both objects are created once with `@State` and passed down. `.task { await shop.load() }` loads the products when the view appears. The product grid reads the state with a `switch`: a spinner, a message with a Try again button, or the grid. `.badge(cart.itemCount)` puts the count on the Cart tab.

The tests use a throwaway `UserDefaults` suite with a random name, so they never touch the real saved cart. They check the cent conversion, that adding twice raises the quantity, that going below one removes the line, and the money format. Money code deserves tests more than almost any other code.
How it works

items: `ShopViewModel.load` fetches and decodes the product list from the service.
Add to cart calls `cart.add(product)`, which updates or creates a line and saves it.
The cart screen reads `cart.lines` and shows steppers. Changes update the total at once.
Place demo order clears the cart and shows a message. No money moves.

The Shop tab shows a grid of products with pictures, titles, prices and an Add to cart button. Add two products: the Cart tab shows a badge with 2. Open Cart: each row has a title, line price, a stepper and a quantity. Press the plus: the total rises. Reduce a line to zero: it disappears. Close the app and reopen it: the cart is still there. Place demo order: the cart empties and says "Demo order placed. No payment was taken." Turn on Airplane Mode before first launch and the Shop tab shows an error with a Try again button.

lessons.title: Project 8: Fitness Tracker with HealthKit and Swift Charts
lessons.description: Build a fitness tracker that reads daily steps from HealthKit, asks permission, draws a weekly bar chart with Swift Charts and tests the progress maths.

content.text: iPhones record steps all day, and **HealthKit** is how an app reads them with the user's permission. This project reads the last seven days of steps, shows today's number with a progress bar toward a goal, and draws a bar chart with **Swift Charts**. Health data is private, so the lesson also shows how permission works and what your app can and cannot learn about the user's answer.

The Simulator has no step data, so the project uses the same trick as the AI chat: a protocol with two implementations. `HealthKitService` talks to the real HealthKit on a device, and `FakeHealthService` returns made-up numbers so you can build and test the whole screen on any Mac.
Concepts in this project

items: **HealthKit capability and privacy text**: add the HealthKit capability and a usage description, or the app will crash when it asks for access.
**Read authorisation**: `requestAuthorization(toShare:read:)`. For read access, iOS does not tell the app if the user said no, so a denied user simply sees zeros.
**HKStatisticsCollectionQuery**: asks for one total per day over a date range.
**Continuations**: `withCheckedThrowingContinuation` wraps a callback API so you can use `await`.
**Swift Charts**: `BarMark` for each day and `RuleMark` for the goal line.
**A fake service**: lets you build and test without a device.

In the Info tab add Privacy - Health Share Usage Description with a plain sentence about why you read steps (see the capabilities note below).

  StepMath.swift         progress, average, goal days
  FitnessViewModel.swift loading state
  FitnessView.swift      summary and chart

The code
**`HealthService.swift`**
**`StepMath.swift`**
**`FitnessViewModel.swift`**

Info.plist keys and capabilities used by projects 8 to 10
(In Xcode: select the project, pick the app target, then Info and Signing & Capabilities.)

Project 8, Fitness (StepTracker)

  Info.plist:   Privacy - Health Share Usage Description
                "Steps are read to show your daily progress. They never leave your phone."

Project 9, Music (MusicPlayer)
  Capability:   Background Modes, tick "Audio, AirPlay, and Picture in Picture"

Project 10, QR scanner (QRScanner)
  Info.plist:   Privacy - Camera Usage Description
                "The camera is used to scan QR codes. Pictures are not saved or sent anywhere."

The other projects need no special capability.
Walkthrough

`HealthService` is a protocol with two functions. The view model only knows the protocol, so it works the same with the real or the fake service. `HealthKitService.requestAccess` first checks `isHealthDataAvailable`, because some devices, such as certain iPads, have no Health data. Then it asks to read step counts. Apple deliberately hides whether the user allowed it, to protect privacy.

`lastDays` works out a start date seven days back and an end date after today, using `Calendar` arithmetic, and builds a predicate for that range. `HKStatisticsCollectionQuery` with `.cumulativeSum` and a one-day interval returns one total per day. HealthKit uses callbacks, so the code wraps the query in a continuation: `initialResultsHandler` either throws the error or returns the list of days. The handler uses `enumerateStatistics` to turn each day's statistics into a `DaySteps`.

`StepMath` holds the three small calculations as pure functions: a progress value that is clamped between 0 and 1, an average and the number of days that met the goal. Keeping them out of the view lets the tests check the edge cases, such as a goal of zero, which would otherwise divide by zero.

The view model has a `State` enum and a `load` function that requests access and then fetches. If anything throws, it shows the error with a Try again button. `FitnessView` receives the service in its initialiser, so the app decides which one to use. In the Simulator, pass `FakeHealthService()`.

In the chart, each `BarMark` uses the date with `unit: .day`, so the axis shows days, and the colour is green when the goal is met. The `RuleMark` draws a dashed orange line at the goal. The `accessibilityLabel` gives VoiceOver users a description of the chart, which is an easy accessibility win.
How it works

items: On appear the view calls `load`. The service asks for access and returns seven days of steps.
The summary shows the last day as today, with a progress bar toward 8,000 steps.
The chart draws seven bars and the goal line. Green bars met the goal.
A line of text reports how many days met the goal and the average.

On a real iPhone, a Health permission sheet appears first, asking to read Steps. After you allow it, the screen shows today's step count in large type, a progress bar, "Goal: 8000 steps" and a bar chart for the last seven days with a dashed goal line. If you walk and reopen the app, today's number rises. With `FakeHealthService` in the Simulator, you see the numbers 4200, 8800 and so on, with the days that reach 8000 in green. The four tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 9: Music Player with AVPlayer and Background Audio
lessons.description: Build a music player with AVPlayer, a playlist, a seek slider, lock screen controls and background audio using the playback audio session.

content.text: A music app has one special need: the music must keep playing when the screen turns off or the user opens another app. On iOS this takes three pieces working together. An **audio session** with the playback category tells the system your app is a music app. The **Background Modes** capability allows audio to continue. And the **Now Playing** and **remote command** APIs show the title on the lock screen and make headphone buttons work.

The player is an @Observable class that owns an `AVPlayer`, so the SwiftUI view only shows the state and sends commands. The track addresses are placeholders: you must supply audio you have the right to play, such as your own recordings or royalty-free music.
Concepts in this project

items: **AVPlayer and AVPlayerItem**: the player plays one item at a time. Replace the item to change track.
**Audio session**: `.playback` lets audio continue with the silent switch on and in the background.
**Periodic time observer**: reports the position twice a second for the slider.
**Now Playing info**: title, artist, duration and position for the lock screen and Control Center.
**Remote commands**: play, pause, next and previous from headphones, the lock screen and car systems.
**Slider editing state**: while the user drags, show the drag position, and seek only when they let go.

Walkthrough

`AudioPlayer` is created once by the view. Its initialiser sets up the audio session, registers the remote commands, starts the time observer and loads the first track. Everything about playback is in this one class, which keeps the view short.

`load(index:)` creates an `AVPlayerItem` and gives it to the player. It also registers for the notification that the item has finished, so the next track starts automatically. The duration is read with `await item.asset.load(.duration)`, which is the modern asynchronous way. If loading fails, the player shows "This track cannot be played right now." That is exactly what you will see until you replace the placeholder addresses.

The periodic time observer runs on the main queue every half second and stores the current position. The slider is bound to that position, but while the user is dragging, the view shows a separate `dragPosition` value. Only when dragging ends does it call `seek`. Without this, the slider would jump back to the playing position under the user's finger.

`configureRemoteCommands` connects the system's buttons to your methods. Each handler returns `.success`, and uses a Task on the main actor because the player is main-actor isolated. `updateNowPlaying` fills the dictionary that the lock screen reads. Update it when the track, duration or play state changes.

The tests cover the time format, including bad values such as negative numbers, NaN and infinity, which AVFoundation can report while a stream is loading. Playback itself needs real audio and a device, so it is a manual test.

Press Play: sound starts and the slider moves. Lock the phone: the music continues and the lock screen shows the title with play and pause. Press Next on the headphones or the lock screen: the track changes. With the placeholder addresses, you see "This track cannot be played right now." and nothing plays. The three tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 10: QR Code Scanner with VisionKit
lessons.description: Build a QR scanner with VisionKit, wrapped for SwiftUI, with camera permission, a result classifier for links, Wi-Fi and text, and safe link handling.

content.text: Scanning a QR code used to need a custom camera pipeline. Today iOS has **VisionKit**, which gives you `DataScannerViewController`: a ready-made camera screen that finds codes and text for you. It is a UIKit view controller, so this project also teaches the bridge between UIKit and SwiftUI: `UIViewControllerRepresentable`.

The most important lesson here is not the camera. It is that **scanned content is untrusted input**. A QR code can contain any text, including a link to a harmful site. The app therefore classifies the result, shows it, warns the user and only opens a link when they tap Open. Scanning needs a real iPhone, because the Simulator has no camera.
Concepts in this project

items: **DataScannerViewController**: scans barcodes with highlighting, guidance and zoom built in. It needs iOS 16 or later and a supported device.
**UIViewControllerRepresentable**: wraps a UIKit view controller for SwiftUI with `makeUIViewController` and `updateUIViewController`.
**Coordinator**: the object that receives delegate callbacks from UIKit and passes them to SwiftUI.
**Camera permission**: a usage description in Info.plist and a request with `AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess`.
**Classifying results**: an enum with link, Wi-Fi and text cases and a pure `classify` function.
**Only http and https**: other schemes such as javascript or tel are shown as plain text, never opened.

The code
**`QRResult.swift`**

**`QRScreen.swift`**

Walkthrough

`QRClassifier.classify` is the safety layer. It trims the text. If the text starts with WIFI: it reads the network name and security type from the fields. Otherwise it tries to make a URL and accepts it only when the scheme is http or https and a host exists. Everything else, including `javascript:` and `tel:` text, becomes plain text. Because the function is pure, three of the four tests need no camera at all.

`ScannerView` conforms to `UIViewControllerRepresentable`. `makeUIViewController` builds the scanner for QR codes only, with guidance and highlighting on, and sets the coordinator as its delegate. `updateUIViewController` starts scanning if it is not already running. SwiftUI calls it whenever the view's state changes, so the `isScanning` check prevents starting twice.

The `Coordinator` implements `DataScannerViewControllerDelegate`. When items are added, it looks for a barcode with a text payload, stops scanning and calls `onFound`. Stopping first matters: otherwise the same code could be reported again and again while it stays in view.

`QRScreen` decides what to show with a chain of conditions. If the device is not supported it says so. If there is a result it shows the card. If the camera is allowed it shows the scanner. Otherwise it explains why the camera is needed and offers an Allow camera button. Explaining before asking improves the chance the user says yes.

On the result card, links show the full address, a reminder to open only trusted links and an Open button that calls `openURL`. Showing the address lets a careful user spot a lookalike domain. Scan again clears the result, which removes the card and brings back the scanner.

A QR code with plain words shows a Text card. In the Simulator the screen says the device cannot scan codes. The four tests pass on any Mac.

lessons.title: Project 11: AI Chatbot App with Streaming Replies
lessons.description: Build an AI chatbot in SwiftUI with streaming replies, a Stop button, saved history, a fake service for testing and API keys kept on a server.

content.text: AI chat is now an ordinary app feature. The user types a question and the answer appears word by word. Building the screen is mostly about state: a list of finished messages plus one message still being written. Building it safely is about design: the AI key must stay on a server, the history sent must be limited, and the user must be able to stop a long answer.

So you can build and test everything without a key or server, the app uses two classes behind one protocol. `FakeAIService` makes up an answer slowly. `ServerAIService` calls your own backend. You start with the fake one and switch when your server is ready. Never put a secret AI key inside an app: anyone can extract it, and you would pay for their use.
Concepts in this project

items: **Protocol with two implementations**: `AIService.reply(to:)` returns an `AsyncThrowingStream<String, Error>` that yields the growing text.
**Streaming state**: finished messages live in `messages`, and the partial reply lives in `streaming`. It is saved only when complete or stopped.
**Cancellation**: the Stop button cancels the task. The stream's `onTermination` cancels the work behind it.
**History window**: only recent messages are sent, because the model has no memory and long requests cost more.
**URLSession.bytes**: reads a response as it arrives, so you can show text before the reply is finished.
**Honest interface**: a notice tells users that AI answers can be wrong.

items: In Xcode choose File > New > Project > iOS > App. Set Interface to SwiftUI, Language to Swift, and Testing System to Swift Testing. Set the minimum deployment to iOS 17, because the code uses @Observable. Name the product AIChat.

Walkthrough

`AsyncThrowingStream` is the bridge between a producer that pushes values and a consumer that loops with `for try await`. In `FakeAIService`, a task splits the answer into words and yields the text so far every 120 milliseconds. `continuation.onTermination` cancels that task if the consumer stops listening, so no work continues in the background.

`ServerAIService` does the same with real data. It encodes the recent history as JSON, posts it and reads the answer with `URLSession.bytes`. Each character that arrives is appended and yielded. The contract with your server is simple: it receives the messages and streams back plain text. The secret key, the choice of model, usage limits and a system prompt all belong on that server.

`ChatViewModel.send` trims the text, ignores empty input and ignores a second send while a reply is running. It saves the user's message, sets `streaming` to an empty string and starts a task that loops over the stream. Each partial value replaces `streaming`, so the screen shows the growing answer with a cursor mark. When the loop ends, `finish` stores the whole answer as an assistant message, saves, and clears the streaming state.

Stop works through cancellation. `stop` cancels the task, the loop ends, and `finish` stores whatever text was received so far. The user keeps the partial answer instead of losing it. An error shows a short message, never the raw error text, because raw errors can leak details.

In the view, a `ScrollViewReader` keeps the newest text in view. The bottom bar swaps the Send button for Stop while a reply is running. The tests check that history is limited, that the fake stream grows, that a finished reply is saved and that empty messages are ignored, all without a network.
How it works

items: `send` stores the user message and starts a task that reads the reply stream.
Each emitted text updates `streaming`, so the screen shows the answer as it grows.
When the stream ends or Stop is pressed, the text is saved as an assistant message.
Messages are encoded to JSON and saved, so the conversation survives closing the app.

content.text: Expected output

The screen shows the title Assistant, the notice "AI answers can be wrong. Check important facts." and an input box. Type "What is Swift?" and press Send: your message appears on the right in blue. An answer then builds up on the left word by word, ending with "Connect the app to your own server to get real AI replies." while the button shows Stop. Press Stop in the middle: the partial text stays. Close and reopen the app: the conversation is still there. Clear removes it. All four tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 12: Video Streaming App with AVKit and HLS
lessons.description: Build a video streaming app with AVKit and an HLS adaptive stream, loading and error states, a video list and playback that pauses and cleans up safely.

content.text: Streaming video is harder than playing a file, because viewers have different networks. A good service stores the same video at several qualities and lets the player switch between them as the connection changes. This is **adaptive streaming**, and on Apple platforms the standard format is **HLS**, recognised by an address ending in `.m3u8`. AVPlayer supports it without extra libraries.

SwiftUI gives you `VideoPlayer`, a view with the standard controls. The part that needs care is the lifecycle: a player holds decoders and memory, so you should stop it when the screen goes away and pause it when the app is no longer active. The project also shows how to watch an `AVPlayerItem` for loading and failure with Combine, so the screen can show a spinner or a clear error.
Concepts in this project

items: **Adaptive streaming**: the player downloads small pieces and picks a quality for each from your current speed.
**HLS**: an Apple format using a playlist file (.m3u8) that lists the pieces. AVPlayer reads it directly.
**VideoPlayer**: SwiftUI's AVKit view with play, pause and a scrubber.
**KVO with Combine**: `item.publisher(for: \.status)` tells you when the item is ready or failed.
**scenePhase**: pause when the app is not active, unless you add background video on purpose.
**Cleaning up**: `onDisappear` pauses and removes the item, which frees memory and decoders.

The code
**`Video.swift`**
**`VideoModel.swift`**
**`VideoScreen.swift`**
**`VideoApp.swift`**
**`VideoTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`SampleVideos` lists two entries. The first is Apple's public HLS example stream, which is meant for developers to test with. Addresses on someone else's server can change or vanish, so replace them with streams you control or have the right to use. The second entry is a placeholder that will fail on purpose, so you can see the error state.

`VideoModel` owns one `AVPlayer`. `play(_:)` creates an `AVPlayerItem` for the chosen video, sets the status to loading and subscribes to the item's `status`. KVO is the older observation system used by Apple's frameworks, and `publisher(for:)` turns it into a Combine stream. When the status becomes ready or failed, the model updates its own state on the main queue. Storing the subscription in `cancellable` keeps it alive, and replacing it cancels the old one.

`VideoScreen` stacks the player, the title and the list. A ZStack puts a spinner over the player while loading and an error message over it when the item fails. The player has a 16:9 shape so the layout does not jump when the video starts. Tapping a row sets the selected video and calls `play`.

The lifecycle is handled in three places. `onAppear` starts the first video. `onDisappear` calls `stop`, which pauses, removes the current item and cancels the subscription. `onChange(of: scenePhase)` pauses the player when the app becomes inactive or goes to the background. Without these, a video can keep decoding after the user has left the screen.

The tests are small because most of the app is framework code. They check the time format, including hours and bad values, and that the sample list contains an HLS address. Playback itself is a manual test on a device or the Simulator with a real network.
How it works

items: Choosing a video creates a new player item and shows the loading spinner.
The status subscription reports ready or failed, and the overlay changes.
The AVKit player handles controls, scrubbing and adaptive quality.
Leaving the screen or the app pauses playback and frees the player item.

Tap "Your own video" in the list: the title changes and, because the placeholder address does not exist, the message "This video cannot be played right now." appears and the app stays usable. Tap the first video again: it plays. Go to the Home screen: the video pauses. On a slower connection an adaptive stream lowers its quality instead of stopping. The four tests pass.

lessons.title: Project 13: Job Portal App with Filters and Resume Upload
lessons.metaTitle: Project 13: Job Portal App in SwiftUI
lessons.description: Build a job portal client with search and filter toggles, a detail screen, a resume picker with size and type checks and a multipart upload.

content.text: A job portal is a good last project because it joins list screens, filtering, forms, file handling and backend calls. It is also close to the purpose of this website. The app has two main screens: a searchable, filterable list of jobs, and a detail screen where the user attaches a resume and applies.

The app can run with no backend, using `FakeJobService` and three sample jobs. When you have a backend, switch to `RemoteJobService`, which expects `GET /jobs` to return a JSON list and `POST /jobs/{id}/apply` to accept a multipart form with a cover note and a file. Sign-in is left out to keep the lesson focused. A real portal would add it with the secure networking pattern from the advanced course and send a token with each request.
Concepts in this project

items: **Filtering with a pure function**: `[Job].filtered(by:)` combines text, remote-only and job types, so it is easy to test.
**A derived list**: `shown` is calculated from the loaded jobs and the filter, so they can never disagree.
**Toggle buttons as chips**: `Toggle(...).toggleStyle(.button)`, with a custom Binding for a set of types.
**fileImporter**: the system file picker. It needs no storage permission and gives access only to the chosen file.
**Security-scoped URLs**: call `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource` before reading a picked file, and stop afterwards.
**Multipart upload**: a text part and a file part joined with a boundary.

content.text: Create the project

items: In Xcode choose File > New > Project > iOS > App. Set Interface to SwiftUI, Language to Swift, and Testing System to Swift Testing. Set the minimum deployment to iOS 17, because the code uses @Observable. Name the product JobPortal.

  JobsApp.swift       @main
  Job.swift           model, filter, sample data
  ResumeRules.swift   file checks, mime type, multipart body
  JobService.swift    protocol, remote and fake services
