The code
**`Job.swift`**
**`ResumeRules.swift`**
**`JobService.swift`**
**`JobViewModel.swift`**
**`JobViews.swift`**
**`JobsApp.swift`**
**`JobsTests.swift (in the tests target)`**
Walkthrough

`Job` is Codable and Hashable, so it can be decoded from the server and used as a navigation value. `JobFilter` is a small struct with the search text, a remote-only switch and a set of types. The extension on `Array where Element == Job` adds `filtered(by:)`. Each rule returns early when a job does not match: remote-only fails a non-remote job, a non-empty type set fails a job of another type, and the search text must appear in the title, company or location.

`ResumeRules.problem` returns a message in plain words or nil. It checks the extension against pdf, doc and docx, rejects empty files and rejects files over 5 MB. These checks give fast feedback, but they are not security. Anyone can send any request to your server without using your app, so the server must check the type, size and content again.

`Multipart.body` builds the request body by hand. Each part starts with the boundary, then headers, a blank line and the content. The file part includes its file name and content type. The last line is the boundary followed by two dashes. Writing it once helps you understand what upload libraries do for you.

`JobViewModel.apply` is where the picked file is handled. The URL from `fileImporter` points outside your app, so the code calls `startAccessingSecurityScopedResource`, and `defer` makes sure `stop` is called however the function ends. It reads the size, applies the rules, reads the data and calls the service. It returns a message instead of throwing, so the view can show it directly.

In the list view, the chips are `Toggle` views with the button style. The remote switch binds directly to the filter. For the job types, a small `binding(for:)` function builds a Binding that inserts or removes a type in the set. The detail view disables Apply until a file is picked and while sending, which prevents double submits.
How it works

items: The list loads jobs from the service and shows those that match the filter.
Opening a job shows its description, a cover note field and a resume picker.
Before upload the view model checks the file type and size and reads the file safely.
A multipart request sends the note and file. The server validates again and stores the application.

The list shows a search field, chips for Remote, Full-time, Internship and Contract, and a row for each job with the title, company and place. Type "kotlin": only the Kotlin job remains. Clear it and turn on Remote and Contract: only jobs that are both remain. Open a job: you see the description, a note box, Choose resume and Apply. Choose a PNG: pressing Apply shows "Choose a PDF or Word file." Choose a PDF under 5 MB: Apply shows "Application sent". With `RemoteJobService` and no backend, the list shows "Could not load jobs." with a Try again button. The five tests pass.

lessons.title: Swift for Android Developers: Kotlin vs Swift, Compose vs SwiftUI
lessons.description: Compare Kotlin and Swift, Compose and SwiftUI, ViewModel and @Observable, Room and SwiftData, coroutines and async/await, with side by side code.

content.text: If you already build Android apps with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, you know more iOS than you think. Swift and Kotlin were designed in the same years by people who read the same papers, so they look alike: both have optionals, data-like types, closures, extension functions and a modern way of writing asynchronous code. SwiftUI and Compose are cousins too: both describe the screen as a function of state, and both redraw when the state changes.

This lesson is a map between the two worlds. It helps in two directions. If you are an Android developer, it shows you where to look in iOS. If you are an iOS developer, it explains what the Kotlin lessons in the Android course mean. It also helps you answer the common interview question: "What are the differences between the two platforms?"
The languages side by side

items: **Constants and variables**: Kotlin `val` and `var`; Swift `let` and `var`.
**Null safety**: Kotlin `String?` with `?.`, `?:` and `!!`; Swift `String?` with `?.`, `??` and `!`. Swift's `if let` and `guard let` match Kotlin's smart casts and early returns.
**Data holders**: Kotlin `data class` gives equals, copy and toString. Swift `struct` is copied by value and gets memberwise initialisers; add `Equatable`, `Hashable` or `Codable` as needed.
**Sealed types**: Kotlin `sealed class`; Swift `enum` with associated values. Both give exhaustive `when` and `switch`.
**Interfaces**: Kotlin `interface`; Swift `protocol`, which can also have default methods through extensions.
**Lambdas**: Kotlin `{ x -> x * 2 }`; Swift `{ x in x * 2 }`. Trailing closure syntax exists in both.
**Extensions**: both let you add functions to existing types.

content.text: The shapes are nearly identical. The biggest practical difference is **memory**. Kotlin runs on the JVM with a garbage collector. Swift uses **ARC**, automatic reference counting, so you must think about retain cycles with `weak` and `unowned` when closures capture `self`. The advanced iOS course has a full lesson on it.
The frameworks side by side

items: **UI**: Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI. `@Composable` functions are `View` structs. `remember { mutableStateOf() }` is `@State`. State hoisting is `@Binding`. `Modifier` chains are view modifiers, and the order matters in both.
**Lists**: `LazyColumn` is `List` or `LazyVStack`. `items(list)` is `ForEach`.
**Navigation**: Navigation Compose with a NavHost is `NavigationStack` with `navigationDestination`. Bottom navigation is `TabView`.
**State holders**: `ViewModel` with `StateFlow` is an `@Observable` class, often marked `@MainActor`. `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` has no equivalent because SwiftUI observes the properties you read.
**Async**: coroutines and `suspend` are `async`/`await`. `launch` is `Task { }`. `Flow` is `AsyncSequence` and `AsyncStream`. `viewModelScope` is a Task you cancel yourself or tie to `.task`.
**Networking**: Retrofit with kotlinx.serialization is `URLSession` with `Codable`.
**Database**: Room is SwiftData (or Core Data). `@Entity` is `@Model`. A Room `Flow` query is `@Query`.
**Settings**: DataStore is `@AppStorage` and UserDefaults. Encrypted storage is the Keychain.
**Background work**: WorkManager is `BGTaskScheduler`. Push is Firebase Cloud Messaging on Android and APNs on iOS.
**Dependency injection**: Hilt is usually plain initialiser injection or the SwiftUI environment in iOS. Heavy frameworks are less common.
**Testing**: JUnit and Compose tests are Swift Testing, XCTest and XCUITest.

content.text: State and screens: Compose and SwiftUI

Both versions are the same idea. The state is owned by the view, the screen is a description of that state, and changing the state redraws the screen. The differences are small: SwiftUI views are structs with a `body` property, and `private` on a @State property is a convention that says the view owns it.
What is genuinely different

items: **Tooling**: Android Studio on any desktop system; Xcode only on a Mac. You cannot build iOS apps on Windows or Linux without a Mac.

**Release**: Google Play takes an AAB and has a review that is usually quick. The App Store needs an Apple Developer account, signing certificates, TestFlight for betas and a stricter human review. Plan more time for iOS review.

**Device variety**: Android has thousands of device models and manufacturer changes. iOS has fewer devices, which makes layout testing easier, but Apple controls which iOS version users run less than you might hope, so always check the minimum version you support.

**Permissions and privacy**: both ask at run time. iOS needs a usage description text in Info.plist for each sensitive feature, and App Store review checks it. Apple also asks for privacy manifests and nutrition-label style disclosures.
**Back button and navigation**: Android has a system back button. iOS uses a back swipe and the navigation bar, so design the flows differently.

content.text: This comparison is from our reading of both platforms and was not tested by building the same app twice. Framework details change every year, so check the current documentation before relying on a specific name.

A good learning path for an Android developer is: read the Swift basics lessons quickly, spend time on ARC and value types, build the Calculator and To-Do projects in this course, and then compare the code with the Android versions. Seeing the same app in both languages is the fastest way to make the two feel like one skill.

The same ideas appear in our other mobile courses. The [Android Development with Kotlin course](/learn/android-development-kotlin-course) builds 21 apps in Kotlin and Compose, and the [React Native with Expo course](/learn/react-native-development-expo-course) shows one JavaScript codebase for both platforms. When you are ready to go deeper on iOS, continue with the [Advanced iOS Development course](/learn/advanced-ios-development-course).
Your task

items: Pick one Android project you built, for example the Habit tracker. Build the matching iOS project in this course.
Write a table of five things you had to change when moving the idea from Kotlin to Swift.
Re-read the ARC lesson in the advanced course and find where your Android code would have needed `weak self`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can name the Swift equivalent of val, a data class, a sealed class, a coroutine, Room and ViewModel.
You can explain why SwiftUI needs no collectAsState call.
You can name two differences in releasing to the App Store and Google Play.

steps.say: Android apps use Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
Both toolkits describe the screen as a function of state and use async code.
iOS apps use Swift and SwiftUI with very similar patterns.
Each ships through its own store, with different tools and review rules.

faqs.q: Can I build iOS apps without a Mac?
faqs.a: Not natively. Xcode runs only on macOS. Some cloud services give you a remote Mac, and cross-platform tools such as React Native with Expo can build in the cloud, but you still need a Mac or a cloud build for the App Store.

faqs.q: Is SwiftUI the same as Jetpack Compose?
faqs.a: They share the same idea: declare the screen from state. The APIs and names differ, and each has its own layout rules, so learn both on their own terms.

faqs.q: Should I learn Kotlin Multiplatform or Swift?
faqs.a: If you want to share business logic, Kotlin Multiplatform is an option, but you still need Swift knowledge for the iOS app. Learning both platforms natively is the safest path for jobs.

Which SwiftUI wrapper is like remember { mutableStateOf() }?

lessons.title: Publish Your iOS App: TestFlight, App Store, CI/CD and Interviews
lessons.metaTitle: Publish an iOS App: TestFlight, App Store
lessons.description: Prepare an app for release, send it to testers with TestFlight, submit it to the App Store, learn what UIKit, Instruments and CI/CD do, and plan a portfolio.

content.text: You now know the language, the screens, the data and the testing. The last step is the one many learners skip: getting the app to other people. This lesson covers the road to the App Store, the tools you will hear about at work, and how to turn this course into something an employer can see. The rules and prices of Apple's programs change, so for each step we tell you what to look for and where, and not a number that may be out of date.
Before you ship

items: **Name, icon and identity.** Choose a name. Add an app icon in `Assets.xcassets`. Check the **bundle identifier**, a unique name such as `com.yourname.expensetracker`.
**Versions.** Each release has a *version* (for example 1.0) and a *build number* that must go up with every upload.
**Quality.** Test on a real device if you can, with different text sizes, Dark Mode, no network, and a small screen.

**Privacy.** If your app collects data, you need a privacy policy at a web address and honest answers in App Store Connect about what you collect. Apple also asks for details about some system features your code or libraries use, so read Apple's current privacy requirements before you submit.
**No hidden secrets.** Remove test keys, passwords and debug screens.

content.text: The Apple Developer Program

To put an app on the App Store, and to use TestFlight with outside testers, you join the **Apple Developer Program**. It has a yearly fee, and you pay Apple. Check Apple's developer website for the current price, the list of countries and what a free account can and cannot do. In Xcode, open **Settings > Accounts**, add your Apple ID, and in your project choose your **Team** under *Signing & Capabilities*. Xcode can manage the signing certificates for you, which removes a lot of the old pain.
TestFlight: beta testing

items: In Xcode choose a generic iOS device as the destination, then **Product > Archive**.
When the archive is ready, open the **Organizer**, choose **Distribute App** and send it to **App Store Connect**.
In **App Store Connect**, Apple's website for your apps, open the app's **TestFlight** tab. Your build appears after Apple has processed it.

Add **internal testers**, people on your own team, who can try the build quickly. For **external testers**, such as friends or a small group, the first build normally goes through a short beta review by Apple, then you can invite people by email or by a public link.
Testers install the free TestFlight app, try your build and send feedback and crash reports.

content.text: The App Store

items: In App Store Connect create the **app record**: name, subtitle, description, keywords, category, support address and privacy policy address.
Add **screenshots** for the device sizes that Apple asks for. Apple lists the sizes in the tool.
Choose the build, answer the age rating and privacy questions, and **submit for review**.

A human and some automated checks review your app against Apple's **App Review Guidelines**. Read them before you start. Many rejections are about incomplete information, crashes or unclear descriptions, and you can fix them and resubmit. Review times vary.

content.text: We cannot promise how long review takes or that an app will be approved. Apple decides, and its rules change. Read the current guidelines on Apple's developer website and keep your first app small and honest.
CI/CD: building automatically
**Continuous integration and delivery** means that a server builds and tests your app every time you push code, and can even upload builds for you. Names you will see in job posts:

items: **Xcode Cloud**: Apple's own service, built into Xcode and App Store Connect. Check Apple's current plans for any free allowance.
**GitHub Actions**: workflows in your repository that can run on macOS machines. Our Git course shows how GitHub works.
**Bitrise** and similar services: hosted build services made for mobile apps.
**Fastlane**: a tool of scripts that automates screenshots, signing, builds and uploads. It often runs inside the services above.

content.text: As a beginner it is enough to set up one workflow that builds the app and runs your tests on every push. That is a strong thing to show.
Instruments and debugging

**Instruments** is a profiler that comes with Xcode. Use it when an app is slow or uses too much memory. The *Time Profiler* shows where the time goes, and *Leaks* shows memory that was never released. Also learn Xcode's **debugger**: set a breakpoint by clicking the line number, run, and look at the values when the code stops. It is faster than printing.
UIKit: the older toolkit you will still meet

Many established companies have apps built with **UIKit**, with screens called *view controllers*, often laid out with **Auto Layout** rules or in **Interface Builder** (storyboards). You do not need it to start, but job posts often ask for it. The two toolkits mix. You can show a SwiftUI view inside UIKit with `UIHostingController`, and a UIKit view inside SwiftUI with `UIViewRepresentable`. A good plan is: after this course, build one small app in UIKit so you understand view controllers, the life cycle and table views, which are the ancestors of `List`.
Turn this course into a portfolio

items: **Expense Tracker**: SwiftUI, SwiftData, a chart (Apple's Charts framework), tests. You built the base in this course.
**Weather app**: REST API, Core Location, loading and error states.
**E-commerce app**: list and detail screens, a cart, sign-in. Use a free fake store API or your own server.
**AI chat app**: call your own server that calls a language model, stream the answer into SwiftUI. Never put the model key in the app.
Put each project on GitHub with a clear README, screenshots and notes on what you decided and why. Anything you can put on TestFlight or the App Store is stronger still.

What to learn next, in order

items: Keep building: one more app each month, a little bigger each time.
Add what job posts ask for: UIKit basics, Combine or more Swift Concurrency, Core Location and Maps, notifications, StoreKit for in-app purchases.
Learn to read other people's code, and contribute a small fix to an open-source app.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay to publish an iOS app?
faqs.a: Yes, publishing on the App Store needs the paid Apple Developer Program. Check Apple's developer website for the current fee and what a free account can do, because they change.

faqs.q: What is TestFlight?
faqs.a: Apple's tool for sending beta builds of your app to testers, who install it through the TestFlight app and send feedback and crash reports.

faqs.q: Do I need to learn UIKit as well as SwiftUI?
faqs.a: Not at the start, but many companies still have UIKit apps, so it is worth learning after SwiftUI. The two can be mixed in one app.
